div.head: POETS AND CHRISTMAS.
div.p: THE POETS AND CHRISTMAS.

Some say that ever 'gainst that season comes Wherein our Saviour's birth is celebrated, The bird of dawning singeth all night long. And then, they say, no spirit dare stir abroad; —The nights are wholescririe ;then no planets strike; ' •No fairy takes; no witch hath power to charm ; So hallowed and so gracious is the time. —SHAILSPEARE,

There let the pealing organ blow, To the full-voiced choir below; In service high and anthem clear As may with sweetness through mine ear Dissolve me into ecstasies, And bring all Heaven before mine eyes. —MturoNi.

Come heap the fagots! Ere we go, Again the cheerful hearth shall glow; We'll have another blaze, my boys ! When clouds are black and snows are white, Then Christmas logs lend ruddy light They stole from summer days, my boys— They stole from summer days. And, let the Loving Cup go round, The cup with blessed memories crowned, That flows whene'er we meet, my boys. No draught will hold a drop of sin If love is only well stirred in, To keep it sound and sweet, my boys— To keep it sound and sweet. —O. W. Hormvs.

(From Ally Sloper's "Christmas Holidays.") • KATE'S SKATE. Let me try now to remember How one icy-cold December I met my darling Katherine—my fate; How dissatisfiesl with sliding, She, with pleasant smile confiding, Besought that I would teach her how to skate. Through all that winter weather Hands clasped we went together, Light glidingat a very rapid rate ; Though freezing fast and snowing, Our hearts were warmly glowing, I taught her how to love as well as skate. It was very aggravating When a thawing stopped the skating, We felt it hard to have a year to wait, And there really were no reasons 'Gainst our loving through all seasons, So hand in hand we mourned we could not skate. Ere the summer spa departed, Blithe Ind gay and happy-hearted, I'd taken pretty Kath'rine for my mate: In my mind there's one thing present— Never banished—'tis too pleasant— One thing I'm ever thinking of— that's Kate.

div.head: RUNAWAY ROMANCE.
div.p: A RUNAWAY ROMANCE.
CHAPTER I.
I am in love. We are both in love.

It has been settled that death alone shall part us. Her Uncle John, however, is ot a different opinion. Her Uncle John is a determined man, and violent. It was he who had the garden wall rebottle-ended. Only last night, as we were bidding each other farewell till next day, she said, "Don't go yet. You are in a.hurry." I had plenty of time for that matter, but I was on the top of the wall on the bottle-ends. I could scarcely help thinking it a little selfish of Rosalind. I could wish, too, Uncle John would confine his opposi- tion to our betrothal to bottle-ends. Its waYking-sticks I can't get used to. -What he said was, "The next time I catch you hang- ing round about my premises I'll lay a stick about your back."
The next time he caught me he did what he had promised.
I ached all over for days and days. CIIA.PTER 11.
The die is cast. We have eloped. Rosalind said, "I can bear this liN no longer." I caught her hand in mine. I said, "Let us away." .She said, "Which way ?" "No matter," I replied.
" Tis immaterial."
She said, " Gretna Green is where they go to in books," and we settled it should be so with us. She then climbed the wall, and, for the first time, realized the bottle-ends.

She said, "I can endure this no longer." I said, "For my sake, Oh, do not." She said. "Can't you see mji frock's caught, stupid ?" Presently (it seemed ages) she freed herself and said, "Catch me, I am going to jump." Rosalind is plumpishly inclined, and I am of slender build. I did all I could at catching her. At any rate I broke her fall. She was vexed : I was hurt. She said she had a great good mind to go home again. I vvish she had. We have done it really now. We have run away. We are round the corner.

We are looking for a cab. We can't find one. I pro- pose a penny tramcar. Rosalind says, "You should have had a post-chaise waiting." By-the-way, I wonder how much post-chaises come to, and how much the fare is from Euston o Gretna, and whether it will run to it.

I could almost wish now we had not been quite so hasty. My idea was the Registrar's office in the parish where we both live. It was thousands to one nobody connected with Uncle John would ever hear of it. But then, of course, you have to wait fifteen days at least. And Rosalind, having run away before ever giving notice,made things a little awkward—very awkward, for that matter.

We are at Euston Station. I find the fare will make a hole in the five pounds (all my ready cash). I shall have to write and ask my employer for a week's leave, and write to my father for an advance when the cermony has been performed—to lend me another trifle. Oh—o !

div.head: CHAPTER 111.
div.p: CHAPTER 111.

I take the tickets, and Rosalind says she is dying for the want of a cup of tea. She must not die. The train we should have gone by if she had not been in fear of death leaves the station whilst the tea is being blown on to cool it. The next train goes this evening. We have seven hours and twenty minutes to wait. We have waited seven hours and twenty minutes. We are both rathet tired.

We have had chops and tea, and been to Madame Tussaud's, and had sherry and biscuits, and made ar exhaustive study of the Ruston Road, and we have had a small tiff—a very small tiff, but yet a tiff undoubtedly: Bosa,lind says she trusts her choice has been a wise one.
We are now about to start by the 8.50, and are on the platform, when Rosalind finds she does not feel at all well. .

There is another train in ten minutes, though. After all, why not catch that? * * * * * WS have missed the nine train too. Rosalind is not even as well as she was. She has gone into a chemist's ' shop, leaving me to buy a newspaper to find out if there is any place of entertainment we might drop into, to 'chile away the three hours before the next train " starts. * Ah hour gone. What on earth hls_beeome of her!
Two hours gone. I have scoured the neighbourhood. I have eorr4ulted a Directory.

I have -Visited every chemist's within a circuit of a mile. I have done it in a cab. What, after all, is the worth of money at a moment like that? What— * * * The deuce The cabman says his fare is five shillings. Two hours and three-quarters since she left. Wha does it mean?
I have just learnt that the twelve o'clock train is an express, and that there is a very serious difference between the fare of the trains. I took the tickets for this one.

If she really does ever come bacKagain at all, how can the excess fare be arranged? , floss me, if there isn't a man from my office. %might as well ask if the letter I sent by a commissionaire to ask 'for leave has arrived safely. He says it has, and that there has been a deuce of a row. He says my father called at the office just when my letter arrived, and my employer said if I did not , return to my duties instantly I should have the sack. This is almost enough to spoil any fellow's honey- moon, I'm blessed if it isn't. - -
Rut what has become of Rosalind ? I did not half like her manner when she left me. She seemed almost as though she wanted to get rid of me. I wish I had waited outside the chemist's shop. _ . _ *
I really begin to think* * * Good gracious! * * * I see it all now. She has been home and told Uncle John. And he is here—with another tralking-stiek.

CHAPTER XXVII. AN. AWKWARD 'COMPLICATION.

_ He had meant to keep away from her but was cheek- mated, as usual. There was some hope of his not succumbing to her irresistible fascination so long as the-two looked at the world through different win- dows. But now she had made a fool of him, as usual. There would be recurrent interviews which could not be avoided, and then that fascination—sleeping like :lightning in the bosom of a cloud, and always mach more attractive to hint in its subtlety and its surprises than mere unchanging physical beauty— would come upon him in full force. She had latterly a sort of horror of too much hand- shaking with the unwashed. Her own experiences had been unfortunate. She had tried to make friends with the cottagers at St-Agatha's—some of whom were still so delightfully picturesque in smock frocks —and even then the experiment had failed. Hitherto she had avoided foul-smelling nooks, where the herd- ing together of the many made civilisation impossible. But one day Fielding came upon her carriage, I stopping before a dilapidated-looking boot-store, en which was written, in large letters, Yes, this is the shop t" and " Never too late to mend." It was just at the time of Ay when the policemen, who are in the habit of chasing small boys, and telling them to "mote on," were comfortably out of the way. And urchins were mobbing the eiegant young lady, who was importing bools tied together by strings as if they were so many sausages, into.her cushioned victoria. "Why did you expose yourself to this ?" he asked her, almost sternly, "I warned you not to attempt it." .

"Oh, I was afraid you would laugh at my abortive efforts to help you, but I noticed that so many of your men and boys wanted new boots." One thing led to another, and he was vexed with himself afterwards for having yielded to her request to let her come one evening, and see him entertain- ing his working friends in the clubroom. He Vicelld have been almost amused if he could have knovin how his wiper had impressed her, aad 114 ti her overrating him ridiculously that night. Such a blending of simplicity and intellectual painstaking Ursula thought she lad never met with in living man berere. The charm of it was thathe Beanie to think he was nothing, and this unconseiousifes of ki§ iiwn Ty-sacrifice made her stand a little ift awe of fn. - - ----: "I content myself with moderate temperature. I have lost my enthusiasm, and can't get hot about anything, since Ray went away," she said rather sadly to Mrs: Wilson, who puazled over this incon- sequent speech, and connected it in a vague way with the typhoid fever which she made up her mind she and _Ursula would catch, in consequence of her charge's latest vagaries. "I shall not displease you if I tell you again what I think ? " Fielding said that night, as he helpea Ursula and her frightened sheep-dog into the carriage.

"Oh, no." "Well, there are too many ladie,a coming here ty fits and starts —it—its a sort of fashion just now. Unless they intend really to live here it does no good. It needs long experience—not impulsive work," She had promised readily enough that slit Would not be hurt, and yet she thought htti imperative and resented his interference7.-he saw it by her quivering lip. It was diappointing advice. And she, who was so ontSpoken . herself, did not like to have the truth spoken to her inso naive a way. Why should he be so determined that she should only give her money, re- fusing to let her fling away a portion of her life as he was so ready to do himself? She gave orders to her coachman without answer- ing as she was inclined to do." Surely you who have such a number of people to attend to—who seem to have taken upon yourself the woes of so many—you, who have so much to live for need not grudge me a little."

----- She knew by this time how he hated to have his actions made much of, and she—who had known enough aggressive flattery herself, and who re- volted instinctively from the first shadow of a com- pliment—was learning to spare him the vexation she dreaded for herself.

He could not actually forbid her from helping him to do good, nor from coming to him for advice.. Yet it was as he had feared. And as time went on this sort of partnership in philanthropy, which he had tried in vain to prevent, increased the magnetic in- fluence which drew these two together by feelings which they mutually shared. If the sympathy could have ended in friendship there would have been no -complications. The, sordid soul makes everything sordid for itself ; the noble soul creates its own sur- roundings also noble, and if life could have flowed on uninterruptedly for these two noble souls they might have beemperfectly happy. But just as Ursula tried to think of Fielding as a friend, and not a lover, telling herself that she would hold him at arm's length if their friendship tried to resolve itself into any nearer intimacy ; so he—who had been longing some time for a companion of his work, a sharer of his thoughts—a second mind in which to lose himself, with common sources of in- terest that should make life fuller and richer—slid by degrees into-the same sort of self-deception. Into this fool's paradise came Louis Grandet, think- ing, as all happy lovers do, that they are the most fortunate of mortal men, till the disenchantment comes, then they: are the most wretched. If he came like a serpent into the garden of Hesperides, he , was a very good-looking serpent. In the interim of the year for 'which Ursula had bid him wait, he had taken more pains than usual with his appearance. Moustache and hair had been carefully traingd as usual, but be had taken to wear the latter longer, and Oscar Wylde himself could scarcely have ob- jected to the coat, which was cut artistically, and set without a crease; while the necktie introduced 6, dainty touch of colour, which had been studied and rearranged before a mirror. If it is one of the first duties in life never to offend the eye of one's neigh- , bours, Grandet could be trusted for never erring in that way. And he had acquired other accomplish- ments ;—he could talk like a good French novel, and had been touring in Brittany to study landscape ' from nature. His character also )aad developed, and when Ursula begged him still to keep their engage- ment secret, saying— " Have patience—we are too young to be married yet," he had for the first time a feeling of uazertainty as to whether the wooing had ever been taken seriously, or whether he could force a love affair, to which Monsieur son ptre and Madame sa mere had officially given their consent. He was still far from the ideal lover, but the year had made more of a man of him, and he had sufficient manliness to resent the fact that Ursula was always quoting "that other fellow's" dictums to him. "I don't understand the charm," he said, exas- perated. It Seemed to him that Fielding was thiowing away his life in the slums of the East-end, and he had never had much admiration for a life spent in active self- sacrifice and endeavour. . .
(To bc continued.)
PART V.

Though the season was nearly wearing itself to a close, Ursula had enough enemies still remaining in town to put the worst construction on the fact that the handsome Frenchman was continually following her about. As she could not prevent his doing so, she had tried not to be sensitive on the point. "The best way," she had contented herself with saying, "will be to thrust the whole tiresome matter out of my thoughts. I can't prevent him from dog- ging me, and I am bound to make the best of it. I have given him my promise." She still thought of the promise as of a tar off thing, which need not be realised yet, and had no idea of making the engagement public scarcely understanding how the matter looked to others, till she overheard the following conversation while she was sitting unnoticed in a tent at a promenade of the Botanical Gardens in July. "Do I know the heiress—Miss Campion? No I certainly do not. My mother takes care only to let us have friends amongst respectable people," said a girl, with amusing pertness. Her companion looked as if he wondered whether she was in earnest or but joking. "She is original," he said, "but I can't quite make her out." _ _

---7`-a17,-Ye-sTshe is much too good company for the men to cut her I but women had much better not be so original. It is most astonishing that any man should want to marry her." "If all reports are true, many have erred in that way," said the other, who scarcely enjoyed the quick retort of the girl. "Oh, but —not now—" And then the voices were lowered, and Ursula understood how the more quickly-judging majority of mankind had decided against her. . It prepared her for what afterwards happened— how the good doctor came down upon her, as she said in "double .quick march," with the idea of looking after her and restoring her to common-sense. "Bless me—what does this sort of nonsenso

mean?" he asked Margaret, with a wistful look in what Ursula would have called his "dear old eyes." "The girl can't keep a couple of beaux going to- gether." He wouldn't "have minded about the one," as he declared to his sister, "though Fielding was the sort of fellow who disappointed one's hopes." He might be head and shoulders taller than other me who had made themselves, and yet never achieve success—" he don't care a fig for success, more's the pity," said the doctor. "He looks a gentleman all over though his clothes may be threadbare. But he will never get on in the world—he is deficient in push," added Dr. Havard, shaking his head, and yet admitting in his secret heart that he was proud of the English race which could produce such men. A new light, which he had the delicacy not to speak about, dawned on him as the explanation of the mystery, when Ursula blushed rosy-red, and declared that she had never dreamt of looking on Mr. Fielding as a "beau." "It is a shame to let him down by calling h'-rn such a contemptible name," cried the girl, indig- nantly. " Hoity toity ! " said Dr. Ha.vard. Then, reflec- tively, "Ah, it is the other, then, and not hs ! " "If you try to be so literal you are sure to be out of it," said Ursula, who was certainly not embar- rassed by his glance this time. "Fact is you will have to come and live near your poor old guardian again. It does not do for hand- some young women to be junketing about in this fashion I' . .

The genial shrewdness of the old man made it im- possible for her to be angry with him, or to remind him that he himself had sent her from S. Agatha's, , When he Went on to lecture her on the lawlessness ' and impropriety of doing such things as she had , done lately in London. "What things ? " asked the girl in righteous in- dignation. The problem became more irritating than ever r when she, with hor spirit up, declared that Fielding's was the "ideal of an occupation," and that she, too, wanted to do somethinr, that was "really useful," and was not to be dissuaded from it by any amount of old-fashioned notions. • Then the doctor stee/td his heart. "My dear, doesn't it strike you that when a marriageable young woman speaks on such subjects to an eligible : young man, when she buttonholes him to listen a hr sympathetic opinions, when she has neither ears or eyelf for other people, when she talks to him— e cohld not proceed with this sort of mental vivisection. He broke off wilp he NAY mounting to the roots of her hair. His face giew`i little darker, but he averted his eyes as if he were watching the folds of her creamy dress, in which lurked varying shades of delicate pearly greys. "This girl is the most extraordinary combination I ever met with," he was saying to himself, as he turned away f rout the strained expression of her f ace, and added in his most stilted speech, "You must be more c,areful,you mustn't get your name mixed up with that sort of thing.." "What sort of thing?" she demanded again, svddenly flashing out: "Wilfred Fielding is my friend.') _

"You can't be in earnest." • tlyhy 5141111n't I mean simply 1114 I hate having fall loii Oil liy Wids." "You are wise in theory, but very, very much wanting in common-sense. Now about the other fellow?"

"Thank you, I have been told before I was un- practical. Theorptically I know women ought not to have secrets, but then life is so difficult, it is not possible to avoid them." You of all people in the ;world I should have thought would be the one to do right in difficult matters without hesitation." . .

"Thank you," she said again. And then slowly, "If I tell you my secret, you will promise me not to let ft out to other people? I promised to marry Louis Grandet when I was almost a child, and I mean to keep my word—l know it was foolish, un- practical, if you will—a promise I should not perhaps have made had I—had I a mother—but unmaidenly —unwomanly—oh no, no." "If you choose to hoodwink yourself," he began, and then seeing that her lips were trembling, though she did not break down, he gripped her hand, and said curtly, "If you had a mother, as you say she might be equal to it, but an old fellow who has lived all his life among books, what on earth do you ex. peet him to understand -about these things?' And he went off muttering to himself, It's the sort of thing women are said to do, but somehow I should not have credited her with such highfiown nonsense."
When the doctor was at all puzzled with the sex, he usually broke off with generalisations about women.

MR. GLADSTONE AT THE EAST END. Mr. Gladstone, on Saturday drove from Westminster to Limehouse to address a meeting of Liberals of the East End. The day was foggy and drizzly. The right hon. gentleman continued throughout the journey exposed to the atmosphere, and by reason of frequent salutations to crowds en route, he was almost continually bareheaded. With him were Mrs. Gladstone, Mr. John Morley, and Mr. Stuart nendel, and on passing through the city there were marked demonstrations of welcome to the right hon. gentleman, knots of bystanders cheering. The meeting was held in Limehouse Town Hall. Mr. John Morley presided. Mr. GLADSTONE, on rising, was enthusiastically cheered. He said he met them with great satis- faction for the purpose of considering at the present moment thoir position in the cause In which they were engaged. It was a great and advancing cause, as was shown by latest intelligence, and that was that Lord Tlartington and a number of other gentlemen had quitted the Liberal Club. (Loud cheers.) All their separations were painful, but it was essential they should look facts in the face. Although what were called Dis- sentient Liberals spoke and voted in favour of the Government, they did not sit with them. No, they remained on the Liberal benches; and the consequence was that when ho looked round for support he did not see the face of a friend, but a foe. There was no use to disguise the truth, which was that there was no political union remaining between Liberal Unionists and the bulk 0r the Liberal party. The real description of the so-called Liberal Unionists was that they were officers without an army, and clergymen without a chinch. He re- garded the result of the Maidstone election as another evidence of the progress which the Liberal cause was making in reference to Ireland. But he wished his audience to look across the sea, where our interests were so great. The Prime Minister had very re- cently made use of an unfortunate expresseet, offensive to millions of our fellow-subject. Nothing could be more absurd than the description of "black man" as applied to the gentleman specially re- ferred to. What was more important wee that in an unfortunate moment of inadvertence, the Prime Minis- ter of this country abould have applied a contemptuous term to the majority of her Majesty's subjects, and having committed that fault in an unhappy moment of forgetfulness, he had not yet offered an apology. We waited for that apology, and the people of India waited for it. The people of India were a people who desired to enter more and more Into the public life of their own country, and their own country was beginning to have a public life. He re- joiced that the principle of loyalty to the Queen and attachment to the English nation and power, never %as so high as it now was, but contemptuous denunciation by the Prime Minister of England were not in the way to Increase that loyalty. After speaking of the sta'e of foreign affairs, and express- ing a hope that Lord Salisbury would avoid complica- tions in regard to the Balkan Peninsula, he referred to the trouble pending at Suakim. Nothing should beguile the people of England or the Government of Egypt into another attempt to conquer the Soudan. Neither Eng- land nor Egypt, he said, had any interest in the deten- tion of Suakim. That principle would, he trusted, guide their policy in the matter. With regard to Parliamentary business, they had an extraordinary condition of things. The Government had arbitrarily abridged the time of private members while wasting the time of the House themselves. After referring to the Irish Question he said, in conclusion, let us persevere in this good cause and this great cause. We are 'cheered on from year to year and from month to month by the hicreasing adhesion of the nation, and we cling to it with our hearts and with our souls, because it is the cause o( honour, it is the cause of loyalty, the cause of patriotism, the cause of strength, the cause of union, and the cause of peace. (Loud cheers.) •

We thought black was the shade for mourning, but now it seems to be for night as well. According to the City Press one 'of the Common Council Candidates has actually been doing his own bill. posting. div.head: POLLING AT COLCHESTER
div.p: POLLING AT COLCHESTER

The p3lling for the election of a representative for Colchester, in succession to the late Colonel Trotter (Conservative) opened on Tuesday, in foggy and frosty weather. The candidates were both about early, con- ducting and superintending final arrangements for the day's.contest. The election excited the keenest interest amongst all parties, but at an early hour little excite- ment was apparent. Many wprkingonen voted during the breakfast hour, but the unfavourable condition of the weather deterred many from hastening to the poll- ing booths. Both parties employed a number of carriages. The nominal electorate is 4,214, but this was much reduced by deaths and removals. Polling proceeded slowly, but as the morning advanced ..became more brisk, and more carriages were employed. As Lord Brooke's carriage, at the close of the Conservative meeting on Monday night, was being drawn to his house, his supporters met those of the Liberal, candidate. Blows were exchanged, and several on each side were hurt. Extra constables were sworn in on Tuesday. The poll was expected to be the heaviest in the history of the borough. The result was declared as follows:— LORD BROOKE (C) 2,126 SIR W. B. GURDON (L) 1,667-439
At the last two elections the figures were 2•- 1889—Trotter (0). 1.96 ; Causton (14, 1.701—5195.

(C), 2,0.4 Causton 44; 1.878-466. Lord BROOK; speaking from his Central Committee. rooms, thanked the electors for placing him at the head rf the poll with so magnificent a majority, knd thanked his opponents for the fair manner in which 'hey had conducted the election. He thought the vie- rory would give strength to the Government He trusted he might for many years look after the interests 'of Colchester in the House of Commons irrespective of !'arty. Sir BRAMPTON GIIRDON also addressed a few words te his supporters from the Liberal Club.
CURRENT POLITICS:
Mr. W. R. Smith, with Mrs. Smith and family, left London on Saturday, for Monte Carlo, yid Dover, Calais. Paris. Sir Charles and Lady Russell also left Lon- don for the same place.

Mr. Gladstone has sent the following reply to a corre- spondent who iriquired of him why he had not yet fulfilled the intention made public by him in n letter dated September 11th, respecting the freedom of Mr. Parnell and other Nationalist members released from Hiltriainharn from complicity with crime :—" December 14th, 1888. Sir,—l find it woute not be possible to produce documentary, evidence in support of my official statement made in 'the House of Commons on May 2nd, 1882, before the Parnell Corn- nrission held its first meeting. I think it inexpedient for me to produce such evidence or in any other way tio re-open the subject elsewherewhile the Commission sits therefore,vraive the intention I had entertained. Lord salisbury was, of course, informed of this change. I now teave the matter as it stands on my public declaration m the name of the Government in May, 1882, which ii, in my opinion, perfectly unequivocal.—l remain, Ste., "W. E. div.head: LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB.

The Pros l Asscclation understands that an intimation has f been received by the committee of the National Liberal Club of the resignation of Lord Hartington, and that his lordship's example has been followed by about 150 other Liberal Unionist members of the club, includ- ing Earl Cowper. the Duke of Devonshire, 'Baron Roths- child, M.P., Sir Henry James, M.P., Sir James MINH., ,M.P., Sir J. Goldsmid, M.P., Sir W. Crossman, M.P., Sir 11. Ilavelook-Allan, M.P., Mr. Fleneage, M.P., Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., and Sir John Fender, M.P. Nearly all the Parliamentary Liberll Unionists have withdrawn, but outside the Parliamentary circle the resignations are comparatively few. The Press Association understands that although Lord Hartington will cease to. be a member of the National Liberal Club after the 31st inst.. he will continue to act as trustee until the annual meeting in May next. In his letter to the committee his lordship expressed a desire .to consult the convenience of the club as far as potseible. The total number of Liberal Unionist secessions up to the present is about two hundred, but it is expected that in the course of the next fortnight about four hundred more members will have followed Lord Hartington's example. Since the announcement cf Lord Hartington's intention an unusually large number of candidates for admission to the club has been nominated, wpwards of one hundred names having been sent in since last Wed- nesday.

FIIAXIM, SATURDAY.—By native opinion the report of the surrender of the Equatorial Provinces to the Mali& 's utterly discreditel. Rad the tribes, it is remarked. gone over t'-e news would have qu'ckly spread over the d an. l'r otamations would have been issued by the Kalifa to tho Emirs and Sheikh+, and instead of a com- placent letter from Osman Digma intimating the fact, the surrender of Suakitn would probably have been demanded. No elation among Osman Digma's followirs ,is visible. The possession of the Khedive's letter is of ' course strong evidence, but it may have been taken from a messenger sent on by Mr. Stanley to Ernin Pasha. This would also account for the Arab's possession of the Snider ammunition. If Etnin Pasha was the Mandi's prisoner it is believed that much stronger proof would have been sent to Ostnan Digma to be cemmunicated to the authorities here. Some European letters of Emin Pasha's would probably have been sent. On the whole, although there is much to cause the gravest anxiety, at present the Ratites story cannot be accepted.

div.head: TIIE KALTFA'S LETTER:.
div.p: TIIE KALTFA'S LETTER:.

Canto, SONDAY.—The following details have been re- ceived of the KaMa's letter to Osmaa Digma announcing the surrender of Emin Pasha and the "white traveller," the contents of which were communicated to General Grenfelli—The Xenia wrote to Osman Digma that he had sent steamers to the equator under the command of Oman Saleb, who reached Ledo, where ke found that Emin Pasha's officers and troops had captured their leader and the" white traveller," both of whom were in chains. They were delivered to Oman Saleh. The latter proceeds to state that the whole equatorial province was now in the hands of the dervishes, and that the people had submitted to the Mandi. Oman sent the chief clerk and the officers to the Kalifs, who received theni kindly. They were, now with him. Oman Saleb's letter to the Kalif°, stated that he reached had.) on the 11th October, and that the Khedive had aent to Fmin Pasha a "white traveller named Stanley," who brought a letter from the Khedive, telling EminsTasha to go with Stanley. Ife offered the remainder of the force the option of going to Cairo, or remaining. They, however, refused to place themselves under Turkish orders, and gbully received Oman. The latter found a quantity of feathers and ivory. Oman Staab heard that another traveller had visited Emin Pasha, but had returned. Prices ruled low, and the supply en greatly exceeded the demand that a great deal of stock was sent back to the country unsold.

Among the living Sovereigns mentioned in the new " Almanach de Gotha." those who have reigned longest ate the Emperor of Brazil, who ascended the throne in 1831, at the age of six; Queen Victoria in 1837; and Duke Ernst of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. crowned in 1844. It is supposed that the child upset the lamp. The neighbours broke open the house on 'discovering the fire, but were too late to save the child's life. TRIS QURFted JOURNEY TO vire" ISA OF Pharr.— In consequence of the thick fog which overhung Wind- sor and neighbourhood yesterday morning, the journey of the Queen and the Empress Frederick to the Isle of Wight was postponed from 9 a.m. until 12 20, when her Malesty left in company with the Empress Frederick and her daughter 4, for Osborne. The rovnl train consisted of seven carriages, including the Queen's saloon. All the royal family wore mourning. It is ex- pected that the Court will remain at Osborne unti-I February, and then return to Windsor.

CIiNrENARTANS.—Mrs. Catherine Hughes, of Madryn, on the estate of Sir Love Jones Parry, has just com- pleted her 101st veer. The old lady is both hale and hearty. 'Sheds slightly deaf, but her memory is unim- paired, and she retains full possession of her conversa- tional faculties—There is residing at the present time in the village of South Thoresbv, near Alford, R man named Thomas Parker, who attained his 101st birthday on the 17th March last. The Lincolnshire patriarch enjoye good health, and is' fairly active. He rises at an early hour every Tuesday morning in order to make the tire and prepare breakfast for his children (aged 71 and 73 respectively) to attend Alford markets

MEMORIAL TO ADMIRAL BLARE AT WESTMINETRR.— On Tuesday morning, Lord Chas. Beresford unveiled the memorial window to Admiral Blake, which has been erected from the design of Mr. Frampton in the Church of St. Margaret, Westminster.—Archdeacon Farrar alluded to the shameful act of removing the great sailor's re- mains with those of other Puritans from Westminster Abbey, and placing them in a common grave in St. Margaret's Churcliyanl. Although one of the founders of the British navy, Admiral Blake had been overlooked by his country, and lie believed the only other memorial of his career • which existed was a bust in his native town of Bridgewater.—Lont C. Beresford unveiled the window, and eulogised the admiral's memory. While in Parliament he took a patriotic line, apart altogether from party, and in addition to great mirage he showed a foresight which enabled him to win his brilliant victories.

Tnit TITHE DurrnAtrirs m FLINTSHIRR.—On Mond..c the distraints for arrears of tithes were continued in Flintshire on an extensive scale by Mr. Stevens, of Lou don, the agent of the Ecclesiastical Commissimers. Accompanied by Deputy Chief-constable Bolton, Inspec- tor Minshull, and a force of police, Mr. Stevens and his emergency men were early at work in the neighbour- hood of flalkin and Ithesycal, where a number of die- traints were levied. Later in the day, and after a brief halt, the scene of operations was transferred to the parish of Whitford, where a large number of distraints were made, among others on the farm of Mr. Edward Jones, Isglan (a prominent tithe agitator and a candi- date for the County Council). At one farm the party were assai with showers of rotten eggs, which proved a most unwelcome attention. The renewal of hostili- ties just row will uhonestionably help the cause of the Liberals and Nonconformists in'reference to the County Council.

THE PHONOGRAPH IN A LAW COURT.—A phono- graph was on Manday, for the first time since its invention, used for legal purposes in a court of law. Jackson and Co., of the United States, wished to register the words "ffo•Ko" as a trade mark for cer- tain goods, the word representing the cry of a species of owl, and being also the war cry of the Chippeway. Indians. The Board of Trade refused the application as this device of an owl had already been repistered for cotton goods. A motion was on Monday made before Justice Kay, and the phonograph was brought into requisition to enable his lordship to hear a perfect representation of the owl's note. The instrument was, therefore, placed on the bench, his lordship expres.ing himself astonished at the.marvellous reproduction of sound. Colonel Gouraud, Edison's re- presentntive, who Was present, conducted an exhibition ot the instrument's powers after judgment was given. INTEMPERANCE CURED.—A wealthy American Lady whose only son was fcr years a slave to intemperance, after seeking In vain for a cure, and trying all known remedies, at last found a simple moans that cured and save him from a drun- kard's grave. Anyone suffering or desiring to help others in this worthy cause, by sending a self-addressed stamped en- velope to Mr. James Holland, 25, Hart•st., High Holborn, London, will receive this information free of charge. Men- tion this paper.—AdvS. The freedom of Waterford was on Wednesday pre- sented to Mr. John Dillon, M.P., in the City Hall. The Mayor presided, and the attendance was very large. MR. GLADSTONE'S DEPARTURE FOR ITALY, &C.—MT. Gladstone, • with Mrs. Gladstone, Mrs. Drew, Mr. Stuart Heade', M.P., and the Misses Rendel, left Victoria Station, London, by the eleven o'clock train on Wednesday morning, for Dover, on his way to Italy. A large crowd assembled at the station to give the Liberal leader a reception, and he was enthusiastically cheered. Mr. Gladstone, who appeared in the best of health and spirits, shook hands with Mr. Morley and other friends on the platform, and another hearty cheer was raised as the ;train moved off. Mr. Gladstone reached Dover shortly before one o'clock. A number of local Liberals were present, and cheered him as he passed to the steamer Invicta, which shortly afterwards sailed. Mr. Gladstone, replying before he left Lcndon, to a memorial from certain unemployed workingmen of London, expresses regret that there is no remedy for the severe distress existing. He points to the difficulty of the House of Commons taking up a local matter unless on a proposal from the Government. Much may be done by employers of labour and the efforts of enlightened personal benevolence, but he looks to the municipal government of London to provide better organisation for promoting the wellbeing of the :labour- ing population.
EXECUTION OF ,THE BIRTLEY MUR.

Wm. Waddell was executed at Durham Gaol, at eight o'clock on Tuesday, for the murder of Jane Beard. more, at flirtley, near Gateshead. The culprit is stated to have slept well during the night, and awakened at half-past five, when he partook of a little breakfast, and appeared cheerful. The officials of the prison soon after- wards assembled, and the Under Sheriff, Mr. Hutchinson, of Darlington, formally demanded the body of the cul- prit from the custody of the Governor, Lieut.-Colonel Armstrong. Meanwhile, Weddell had been removed from his cell, escorted by two warders and Berm, the executioner, and taken to the press-room, where he was pinioned. He showed decided signs of mental se- nds!), but he walked firmly to the scaffold, and submitted to the final offices of the executioner without exhibiting any feeling. The customary procession accompanied the culprit, there oling in addition to the prison officials, four reporters. Waddell once only placed his hand on the arm of a warder, as if needing support, hut quickly steadied him- ;elf, and walked to the drop without again faltering. che chaplain offered up a final extempore prayer, Berry drew the bolt, and the culpritdied apparently without a nzuggle. The arrangements were so bad that the Pres.; representatives present practically saw nothing of the execution. A drop of about six feet was given. Berry r•lept in the prison all nicht. About 100 persons were present when the black flag was hoisted. Win. Waddle, convicted of the murder of Jane Beat- more, at Birtley, made a full confession of his crime on Sunday afternoon. The Dean of Durham received a request to visit the prisoner, but, having no authority to enter the prison, he wired for permission to the Home Secretary and obtained it. The very rev, gentleman at once proceeded to the gaol in his carriage, and Waddle made a fall confession to him. /t is impossible to give details of the confession. Some of them are shocking.

div.head: COTTON MILL BLTENT AT BACUP.- A MAN SUFFOCATED.
div.p: COTTON MILL BLTENT AT BACUP.- A MAN SUFFOCATED.

Shortly before five o'clock on Monday afternoon, a fire broke out in the serond story of an extensive cotton waste mill at Pippin Bank, Bacup, belonging to Mr. Jas. Flargre.aves. The mill is four storeys high. Owlng to the very inflammable nature of the contents, the fire .nread with alarming rapidity, and hi a very short time he whole building was in flames. As the flames soon got a firm hold, no • hope was entertained of OnVitlß he building, and all efforts were directed towards oreventlng thel'spread of the conflagration. The Rawtenstall fire engine was telephoned for, and arrived About six o'clock, and was followed by the Whitworth tire engine. Some hand manuals belonging to neigh- bouring mills were got into action before the arrival of the fire engines. 'file roof fell in about six o'clock, and the inhabitants of dwelling-houses in the vicinity began to remove their furniture, as it was feared the firs ,vould extend, owing to a favourable breeze which was blowing at the time. The enginee and other appliances lid good service, although they were short of water, and the flames were rot under about seven o'clock. The fire- men continued to play on the horning loess all night. As the flames were visible for miles around, a crow4l which numterrd several thousands fathered. Art ekierly ran, named William Lord, who was employed in the top storey, lost his life. When the fire broke out, a 'ming man, named Jesse Briggs, went to look for him. and got him on his back, but on arriving at the second Amoy, where the fire .was raging fiercely, he was corn- tolled to lay down his burden to save his own life, and the old man was not seen afterwards The origin of the ere. is not known. The damages are eartly covered by insurance. The building was completely gutted, and but a very small portion of the stock was saved. The damages amount to nearly .£B,OOO, about one-fourth of \silken is oveted by insurance. The body of the man wa found in the ruins on Tuesday morning, very little burnt, death apparently being due to suffocation,

div.head: WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE .
div.p: WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE .
CONCERT.

The 18th annual concert in connection with Warrington People's College WAS given ill lb@ Public Hall, on Tuesday evening, by the pupils. There was, as usual,a very large attendance,the hall being filled in every part, most of those ' present being parents and relations of the scholars. The hall had been tastefully decorated. by Mrs. O'Brien. with banners and flags around the front of the galleries, and plants, from the conservatories of Mr. John Crostield, on the platform. The first part of the programme consisted of Mr. T. Mee Pattison's cantata, " Sherwood's Queen," the principal eh exacters being allotted as follows :—Robin Hood, George Smith; Little John, Jullien Wilson; Allan- a-Dale, Fred Clarke; Will Scarlett, George E. Clay; Friar Tuck, Frank Stringer; Alice, Miss Mary Williams; Marian, Miss Clara Dinwiddie; Widow, Miss J. Ada Wright. These performers, as also the numerous foresters and maidens, were all dressed in character, the get-up of Friar Tuck being particularly amusing. The chorus consisted of a large number of scholars all of whom were brightly and neatly dressed. The cantata was excellently rendered, the youthful soloists being parti- cularly deserving of praise. Pile second portion of the Programme included as choruses "The Old Brigade," "Vocal Waltz on Old English Melodies," "The Hurri- cane Chorus,"' Sweet is the Murmur" and "The Mariner's Song." A solo and chorus from "Ruddigore " was also given, George Smith acting so efficiently as the soloist that he was warmly recalled.. An amusing des- criptive chorus by Messrs..W. H. Wallington, W. Brown, C. Corlett, Podmore,and Smith was very highly enjoyed, and these performer t received a well-deserved encore. Jullien Wilson likewise did well in the solo and chorus, "Trial by Jury." The whole concert from a musical, as from other points of view, was a decided success, and was in every way creditable to the conductor, the Rev. E. Moore, Mr. Twis.s (headmaster), Mr. Wallington, and the others who took an active part in arranging and carrying it out. Mr. T. Mee Pattison it is needless to say, made a most efficient organist. in the interval. Alderman Davies, who presided, said he had been requested, and it was a great pleasure to him, to make the presents that evening. The very handsome books they saw before them were to be presented to 41 children who had never missed once during the session. They *mild easily understand what a difficulty it would be in a large school like that to give to those who really deserved and yet to avoid, giving disappointment to those who were, so to speak, very near the gcal, and, therefore, they had determined that the books should be given to those 41 children who had never missed once. The presents had been purchased out of the school funds, so that they could well understand that the school was rich enough, through its own industry, to be able to give those valuable prizes to the children. The parents, feeling so heartily the education that was being given to their children, had subscribed for two desks which would be given to two of the teachers—Miss Plinston and Miss Wright, who nad got Queen's prizes, which he hoped would be of more use to them than even the desks. (Applause.) Alderman Davies then presented the books for regular attendance to the 41 scholars alluded to above. After this had been done, he Said his heart was full, and he was sure there weremany fathers and mothers there that night who felt their hearts full to see the children assembled together. Remarking that he had been born sadly too soon, Alderman Davies went on to give some amusing reminiscenes of the manner in which instruction was imparted when he was a lad. Those days had, however, gone by altogether, and the children who were taking part in that evening's entertainment were receiving such an education as was never dreamt of in days gone by. (Hear, hear.) When they considered the education which the children were getting they could not help feeling that they had a bright future to look •forward to in this country. . (Applause.) Some forty or fifty years ago great progress was made in education, bit children had far superior advantages now. If, how- ever, it were not for the persever4nce and determination of men like Mr. Twiss and his assistants, to do the very best they could for the children, all the forms and ceremonies of schools would be as nothing. . (Applause.) He would now call upon Mr. John Crosfield, pm., to read the report. Mr. J. Ceosrietn, jun., then read the report as follows :—As Secretary I have again the pleasure of saying that the People's College has had another most successful year. There has been a considerable increase in numbers. With the view of making the teaching as thorough and successful as possible, the staff was in- creased last Christmas by the addition of two certificated teachers—a master and mistress—thus making no fewer than twelve certificated assistants, besides nine pupil teachers, and special teachers for sewing, singing, and drill. The confidence ot the town and neighbourhood in the management of 'the school has also been mani- fested by her Majesty's Inspector and the Education Department. You all know how difficult a thing it is to get money from the Government without a well- merited equivalent, yet so uninterrupted has the succes.s of the school been for years, Viet, on the recommenda- • ' tions of Her Majesty's Inspect*, the grant has been paid without examination, a very rare occurrence and the highest compliment that any school could receive. In passing I cannot help saying that it is a pleasing thing to find that in our comparatively small town another school—the Parish Church Boys'—has received the same gratifying honours. I believe there is only one other school in the whole of Mr. Harrison's district that has been so complimented. I think you will agree that this speaks well for Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The pupil teachers have maintained their usual excellent position at the collective examination held in April. At the examination for admission to the training colleges Miss Amy Plinston; of the main school, and Miss Ada Wright, the of Cairo-st. Infants', who completed their apprentice- ship as pupil teachers, each gained Queen's scholarships of the first class and will enter the training college in January. The average attendance for the year was increased to 735 including the ex. standard VII., and there are at present on the books over 880. Of this number 380 are in the three highest standards V. VI. VII., which make the heayfest demands upon a teacher's ability, tact, and resources. The higher branches of education have received increased attention throughout the year. Drawing, mathematics, anddemestic economy

have been carefully and systematically taught and in order to prepare the way for youths to avail themselves of &asses for technical and scientifie instruction, if such ever be established in the town, another master has been engaged for the higher standards so that these subjects may be still more thoroughly taught. As the scholars were not examined H.M. Inspector's report refers only to the pupils teachers, and to a suggestion in reference to the cooking. It is as follows: •By mynext visit I shall hope lo find special and appropriate provision made for the teaching of cookery as recommended last year. The papers worked by the pupil teachers are again, generally speaking, quite first rate, and might serve as models of what the working of such papers should be. All the pupil teachers—A"Knowles, J. A. Bunch, C. J. Owen, J. Bowen, A. A. Plinston, M. Williams, M. A. Sewards, M. Butterworth, and C. S. Dinwiddie have passed well Mr. Richardson, Mr. Burton. Mr. Ward, and Miss Broom- head will receive their certificates in due course." In conclusion I should like to read a paragraph in reference to our school contained in the report of H.M. chief Inspector of schools for the North-Western division of England, and to be found in the Blue Book for 1887 issue in September last. Mr. Coward says :—One of the best schools I have ever seen, the British school, Warrington (People's College) is a mixed school and has for many years been doing most valuable work and is in reality supplying a, thorough good commercial education ito all n the neighbourhood desiring it,and willing to pay the fee. There has beem no difficulty arising out of it peculiar organization, and not even those jealous of its success hays been able to make out any case against it. But the master is a man of unusual energy, vigilance,and i resource, and every proper precaution s taken to adapt the organization to meet the needs of the case." . Alderman DAVIES observed that the school was so 'se-client that the Inspector had not thought it necessary to have an inspection at all. (Hear, hear.) When he told them that there was another school in the town in a a similar position, and that those two Warrington schools were two out of three in that state in the whole district, it would be seen that they had reason to be proud of their schools. (Applause.) He could not sit down without asking them to express their appreciation of the excel- lent music which had been rendered that evening, and of the efforts of the Rev. Edward Moore, assisted by Mr. ' Edward Wallington, who had brought the children up to the state of perfection in which the audience .found them. (Loud applause.) At the conclusion of the concert, Mr. F. Monks moved a vote of thanks to Alderman Davies. They would notice, he said, that the Inspector, in his report, laid great stress upon the desirability of cookery being added to the other subjects taught in the school. The Committee had therefore decided that if they met with sufficient support a cookery school should be started. (Applause.) No part of the present funds was available for building pur- poses, but the Committee could provide the necessary appliances and things of that sort out of the funds of the school. If, then, their friends would subscribe a matter of £2OO with which to build a suitable room in which 70 or 80 pupils could In taught at one time, the Committee were prepared to do the remainder out of the funds at their disposal. (Applause.) He was sure they would agree with him as to the importance of teaching girls cooking, as well as sewing and other things, and he believed the matter had only to be mentioned and the object explained to bring h the necessary subscriptions. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Alderm in WEasiaa seconded the proposition. The vote of thanks was heartily accorded and Mr. DAVIES, in responding, called for cheers for Mr. Twiss, Mr. T. Mee Pattison, the Rev. Edward Moore, Mr. E. Wallington, and others which were heartily given. Mr. Monks mentioned that next year would be the jubilee of the school. The singing of the National Anthem brought the meeting to a close. The following is a list of the children who received prizes for regular attendance throughout the year— not having beer. absent a single time :—Boys Ex.—St. VlL—Charles R. THREATENING TO IMITATE " JACK THE RIPPER."— Edwin Bibby, joiner. Albert-terrace, Stockton Heath, was brought up under a warrant charging him with having on the 15th December assaulted his wife, Sarah Ellen Bibby.—The complainant said her husband came home drunk on Saturday night. He at once without the slightest provocation, began to illuse her. He took hold of her by the hair and struck her a violent blow in the face with his fist, discolouring her left eye. He took up the poker, but did not strike her with it. He said he would kill her, do away with Ler, and rip her up. Witness gave him his shirt., and he threw it on the fire, and said he would put her there as well. He said it would not take him more than three or four minutes to rip her up and if Jack the /tipper did not do it he would. They had been only married twelve months, and complainant had four children by a former husband. The youngest was eleven years of age. She asked for a judicial separation, as life with the prisoner was simply unbearable. His wages were 30s. a week.—A lodger named Mrs. Jukes gave corrobor- ative evidence as to the vssault.—P.S. Booth said that he was passing the house about 11 p.m. on Saturday, and hear; log cries of " Murder" went in and saw the prisoner Musing his wife.--The prisoner denied assaulting his wife, and said she aggravated him by always presisting in having the last word. He had no comfort at home. On Saturday morning he had to go to work without his breakfast.—The Bench considered the charge fully proved, and imposed a fine of 10s. and costs. They also granted a judicial separa- tion, and ordered the prisoner to pay 10e. a week towards the maintenance of his wee. - .

LIBRAL CLUB SMOKING CONCERT. On Saturday evening a largely-attended and enjoyable smoking concert was held at the Liberal Club, Bewsey-st. The President of the club (Councillor Fleming) occupied the chair, and amongst these present were Councillors F. A. Roberts and W Pierpoint, Messrs. T. Morris, A. Browne, C. J. Holmes, Are. In a few opening remarks, the chairman • expressed his gratification at seeing so many present at their first smoking concert. It might be said that in starting those concerts they were following the example of the Conservative party. In a sense no doubt they were following them, but it was an idea he had had in his head for some time. He was gratified they had made a start, and he felt quite certain that this would not be the last, but that the concert would be followed by others of a larger and more influential character. (Applause.) It was said that the Liberal Club encouraged drinking and gambling, but he wanted them to understand, and the town of Warrington to understand, that nothing of the kind was eecouraged. As far as drinking was con- cerned, the state of affairs was quite different to what it was reported to be, as the receipts for the sale of intoxicating liquors were only a fourth of the amount received at the bar, the bulk being for coffee, cigars, and other like refreshments. (Hear,* hear, and applause.) That being the case he thought they were proceeding in the right direction, and he should like the youths of the town to be present as often as possible, their seniors would also be present, and that fact would be sufficient to deter them from drinking and gambling. (Hear, bear, and applause.) A comic song, 'Biddy dear," was given by Mr. .Whitehead in such a fashion that he was warmly re- called, and then gave "What Sergeant Cox told Monaghan," with 'equal success. ' Mr. A. Cavanaglr admirably rendered "The Village Blacksmith," and on being encored gave "The Friar of Orders Grey." Mr. Littlewood's singing of "The White Squall" was also a great success, and he had again to oblige the audience by a rendering of It was a dream." After an interval of a few minutes, Mr. TnomAs Mourns gave a short address. He thought all present would agree with him that Councillor Fleming had acted very wisely in starting these smoking con- certs, which would, le believed, be a most excellent thing for the club. He had never met amore appreci- ative audience since he had been in Warrington, and that was a matter which reflected credit upon them. The Chairman had made a remark to the effect that people outside said the Liberal Club consisted of a great many gamblers and drinkers. He contended that of all clubs where drink was sold this was the mmt sober club of any which existed in the town. (Applause.) With regard to the gambling question, he might say that he was chairman of the Warrington Cocoa and Coffee Com- pany, and they had not started the company more than three months before he was seized upon by two or three persons, who said theirlads had commenced to gamble. If they would gamble in a cocoa room, they would surely gamble here and elsewhere., The word "gambling" required a definit'on. He contended that if a man gambled for a penny, or a youth played cards for the same amount, he was just as much a gambler, if he could not afford to pay the penny, as a man on the turf who lost £l,OOO, and went off without paving £lO. (Hear, hear.) No man should play for a stake unless he could afford to lose it. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Morris also spoke against excesses of other kinds, and called for three rounds of applause for their Chairman and they were heartily given. The second part of the programme consisted of a song "The Wolf," by Mr. J. Giblains ; a duet, All's well," Messrs. Littlewood and Gibbins ; song. "When other lips," Mr Littlewood ; a comicsong," Massha toori ra," by Mr. E. Whitehead, all of which were very excellently rendered. Mr..l. 13. Caldwell, it is needles,: to say, made a most efficient accompanist. A brief address was also given by Councillor W. rierpoint.

; because "the exigencies of a great political party are sometimes extreme." Possibly so; but may it not be that the leader of the Liberal party is now free, to move because he is rid of such weak-kneed Liberals as the member for ' Rossendale and his followers ? One motive is as likely as the other, and it is not improbable that the advance is the result of the conjoint tigtion of uoih influettces. It is something that it 10. advance, and that Lord Heatii{dMil ,411:1348 0114 _ he is left behind. And this being the case, how about his relations with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN ? Will the member for West Birmingham still speak of Lord lI.A.RTINGTON as his leader, now that the Liberal party have included the chief features of the "unauthorized programme" which was once, professedly, so dear to nis heart? It will be interesting to observe, when Mr. CHAMBERLAIN returns from the clouclland of his honeymoon, whether he will be content to beat time and roll logs with the member for Rossendale. If he does, he is doomed as a politician; it will be another striking instance of arrested development. He will be classed amongst those who have gone to sleep; he will be ticketed as belonging to the family of the Rip Van Winkles.

What may be regarded as a final judgment has at Length been pronounced in a licensing case of which a good deal was heard when the question was before the country of compensation to publicans and brewers. It will be remembered that the Government based their proposal to give power to County Councils to grant compensation to pub- licans on the assumption that the holder of. a license had a vested interest in that license, seeing, it was asserted, that licensing justices had no power to refuse the renewal of a license, except in case of misconduct. It was in vain that eminent lawyers and laymen proceeded to show that this was a doctrine which had no foundation in Acts of Parliament. The Government held to their opinion, until there was such a storm about their ears that they were glad to save their official lives by throwing over this portion of the Local Government Bill. During the controversy, what is known as the Kentmere licensing case was referred to as an instance of magis- trates refusing to renew a license, and of their refusal to renew being sustained not only by the Court of Quarter Sessions, but by a Divisional Court of the Queen's Bench. It was reported that, the case would be carried to the Court of Appeal; and the next that was heard_ of it was that the appeal had been abandoned as hopeless. It was, wever, taken to the Court of Appeal, where judgment was pronounced on satnr- day. The particular issue %Is whether the magis- trates were legally entitled to refuse to renew the license of a public-house known as the Low Bridge Inn, Kentmere, on the grounds of "the remote- ness of the inn from police supervision, and the character and necessities of the neighbourhood." The Master of the Rolls (Loan ESHER) delivered an exhaustive judgment in which he dealt with the various Licensing Acts bearing on the subject, commencing with the Act of 1828. He acknow- . _ ledged tuelarg; nterests involved in the ques- tion—for it j _e_,nessary to say that a decision of this kind affects, some millions of capital—and said he had listened with care to the arguments adduced in support of the appeal. His decision was that the appeal must be dismissed with costs; and in this decision Mr. JUSTICE DAY and Mr. JUSTICE LOPES concurred. LORD ESHER said :—".[n the absence of any legislative declar- ation to the contrary, he mist hold that the Act of 1828 gave the justices unlimited discretion in all matters relating to the granting of licenses." Again:—" He did not see why the magistrates in granting a license might not act according to their own knowledge of a neighbourhood, and in exercising their discretion they might bring that knowledge to bear. In such a position their dis- cretion was unlimited." Mr. JUSTICE DAY said : 'ln the case of the Queen v. Lancashire Justices, Mr. Jusnca WILLES laid down the principle that the justices consider all the merits of an applica- tion apart from the conduct and character of the applicant himself; they could take into consider- ation the questions of locality, population, and the number of houses already in existence. He quite agreed with that opinion, and must say that it was consistent with the strict letter of the law." It may be asked, since the law seems clear upon the subject, how it happens that the issue has been contested so stubbornly. As to this it may be remarked that the custom, generally speaking, has been to renew a license where no misconduct has been shown. As the law now stands, a license- holder must have notice that objection will be taken to the renewal of his license; otherwise he need not attend the Licensing Session. It was thought by those whose wish was father to the thought that this gave a prescriptive title to the license, and "the trade" is so rich that it could well afford to fight a legal battle of this kind. It has fought, it has lost; and the result is a revelation of what the countrphas escaped by refusing to be party to the compensation clauses of the Local Government Bill. If those clauses had been passed, license holders would have had for the first time a legal title to a vested interest which is now found to exist in the imagina- tion only; and the nation would have been liable to claims amounting to hundreds of millions of money. There is no possibility of any such monstrous legislation now, in view of the judg- ment of Saturday last. Further, licensing magis- trates who believed their hands were tied, are now informed that their hands are free; they are at liberty, without any local option Act, to reduce the number of licensed houses as they may think fit. Their discretion is absolutely unlimited ; and if they do their duty at the next licensing sessions they will, at the very least, rid the country of the "dens of infamy" which are a source of so much trouble to the police, of cost to the community, and of evil to tho inhabitants.

. A mean and ridiculous attempt has been made to discredit Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., through his can- nection with Messrs. BRUNNER, MOND and Co. Tile accusation appears in the "London Evening New," a Tory journal, and the chief accuser is a Socialist of the name of CHAMPION. It is stated that Mr. BRUNNER is one of the proprietors of the London " Star"—a new journal which, as an organ of Radicalism, has had great success in the metropolis. That, no doubt, is the head and front of Mr. BRUNNER'S offence; he has assisted in establishing a Radical paper which has already left the Tory paper a long way in the rear. Mr. ' CHAMPION as a Socialist has made a mull of it in attacking Mr. BRUNNER. All he can say is that workmen are fined and dismissed at the works of Messrs. BRUNNER, MOND and Co. for what is stated to be trifling neglect of duty. Mr. BamiNzn, as it happens, has not had to do with either the taking on or discharging of a single ! workman; that is a department of the business with which he has nothing to do. But that would not save him, if such petty tyraimy was exercised at the works as is alleged
THE EXA

r against the foremen and managers. People would soon say—" Like man like master," and Mr. BRUNNER VFOUId be in disrepute. As to whether this is so or not, the elections in which he has taken the principal part are the best test. When he was elected to represent the Northwich Divi- sion, in 1885, his majority was 1,028; and when he was re-electe4 last year it was 1,129. Now, , how could this be, if the workpeople were mused? Ti titti yfcrg badly paid or otherwise badly treated at the works, they uld be sure to revenge them- selves at the ballot-box, where:they ;'nuld retell with impunity. So far from dismissing men, or driving them away by fines, it is the boast of the firm that they employ almost every man who started with them when the works were com- menced in 1873. If Mr. BRUNNER had been indifferent to the condition of the working classes, he would not have spent £5,000 in erecting a Free Library for Northwich; nor would he have con- tributed largely to the Widnes Library; or have assisted the down-trodden tenants of Ireland with a contribution of £l,OOO. The fact is Mr. CHAMPION has been talking about that which he knows nothing; and has succeeded—not in injuring Mr. BRUNNER but in making himself look ridicu- lous. Let him come to Northwich and give vent to the "grievances" of the men; he will find him- self answered very quickly; and will go back to London with a bee in his bonnet.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

A Merry Christmas to everybody! It is not everybody who will be merry, but it is some- thing towards it to know that trade is, on the whole, better than it has been for several •seasons ; and that means material comfort, which is one of the foundation, stones of merriment to the classes and the masses.

The old couplet has it : At Christmas ptay, and make good cheer„ For Christmas comes but once a year. And it is an old couplet. It was written by Thomas Tusser, who had being from 1523 to 1580. Tusser has been dead these 300 years; but his lines are like John Brown's soul ; they go "march- ing on."

The Liberal Unionists are leaving the National Liberal Club; but no harm will come of their desertion; the club will be there when they are gone. They are making way for better men, for there are hundreds of sound Liberals ready to take their places.

It is rumoured that Mr. Smith—he of the House of Commons—is to be " promoted "to the House of Lords, after he has had his little holiday. He will require a title, of course. How would Baron Bookstall be? It has a good sound with it, and it is in bitrmony with the eternal fitness of things.

There is still hope of Stanley turning up safe, sound, and free. The Emin Relief Committee at Berlin have come to the conclusion that the story told by the Arabs is altogether unworthy of credit. Lieutenant Wissmann will therefore set out for Africa as soon as possible. We may yet be able to exclaim with fervour "On Stanley, on

We are compelled, under the unusual pressure upon our space, to leave over until our next issue, several letters, and items of news, including account of the experiment yesterday at the Howley Daptit, and report of meeting, last night 91 the Economic" Building Bociil23„

It 'matter of course for constables to toe the line • but how when they get " over the line ?" A round half-dozen of Warrington constables have been suspended—so it is rumoured—for being too "elevated" for their lowly duties. Are there more pare " in the borough than the average police- man can safely pass? Or is it that some• of the force have been Christmasing too early, and too much?

The Warrington literary and Philosophical Society are providing, this winter, a series of lectures which is rather above the high average. What is needed, in addition, is that the members should contribute by criticism at the close of a lecture. It would show an intelligent interest in the Papers, and give life to the proceedings. The Chairman for the time being should try to bring the members out.

There is a rumour cureent that the county magistrates are about to forestall their successors— the County Councillors—by granting a retiring pension of £BOO a year to the Chief Medical Officer of Rainhill Asylum. If the justices do anything of the kind, they will certainly prove themselves to be what they are sometimes styled—an "irrespon- sible body of men." In that case the asylum itself would be the fittest place for them.

The Law of Libel Amendment Bill is now safe, thanks to the careful pilotage of Sir Algernon Brothwick. This does not mean that it will now be safe for the prep to practice libel; the indivi- dual is still protected; but—what has hitherto been lost sight of—the press is in some degree protected too. We are believers in "protection" when protection for one person can be had without injury to another.

It must be gratifying to John Bright, as he lies on a sick bed, to receive messages of sympathy from all sorts and conditions of men. Liberals'are not forgetting him; they can forgive his recent hard words on the Irish Question, for they remember how eloquently in the past he pleaded for justice to Ireland. May he live to see that Home Rule ip as safe as he thinks it is dangerous!

The Panama Canal Company is in difficulties, and there is considerable excitement in France. It is really bankrupt, but bankruptcy is an ugly word, and Frenchmen do not like to associate it with the name of brave M. De Lesseps. An effort is being made to help him' but we do not see how it is to succeed. The Canal is likely to prove the grave of the last sixpence for many poor shareholders.

We seem to be paying dearly at present for the making of the Ship Canal. There is a considerable number of men in the hospital at Thelwall suffer- ing from accidents of various kinds; and on Satur- day afternoon two men were killed through an engine running off the line. It is noteworthy that an accident with an engine happened the other week, at Walton, on a Saturday afternoon. Can it be that the men are off guard at pay time? The matter is worth inquiring into. It is sad to hear of these lives being Jost.

Advt SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN STATION.— A married woman, named Mary Ellen Hunter, residing at 7,.Rockwood-st.' Liverpool, met with a serious accident at Earlestown railway station on Friday • night, and narrowly escaped a shocking death. Mrs. Hunter arrived from Liverpool in the afternoon on a visit to her husband, who is employe I at Messrs. Vicar's works, and lodges at the house of Mr. Samuel Moss, Earle-st. She and her husband booked for Liverpool by the 97 p.m., but for seine reason did not proceed by that train. About twenty minutes past ten they together crossed the lines to the Liverpool side, and at that moment the 1022 train for Liverpool came in. Mrs. Hunter was just stepping on to the platform when the engine caught her a severe blow and she was knocked to the ground, fortunately falling on the platform. She was placed on the seat of the waiting-room, and Dr. Hardyside was sent for. The woman was taken home, and on the doctor examining her he found three of her ribs were broken and she was otherwise bruised. She was removed to her home at Liverpool on the following day, and has since continued to make satisfactory progress towards recovery.
