div.head: ALLEGED ATTEMPTED MURDER BY A FATHER AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED ATTEMPTED MURDER BY A FATHER AT WIDNES.

I At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Michael Sweeney, of 13 Peel-st., was charged with having attempted to murder his daughter Ellen Sweeney. Margaret Roach, daughter of lhomas Roach, of 13 Peel-st., deposed that on Tuesday night she saw Ellen Sweeney come from the house and faint in the street. Her mouth was much swollen.—lnspector Keighley said he visited the house on Wednesday. He slw the girl in bed and she stated that she received her injuries through her father striking her. Her lips and neck were much swollen, and there were marks of violence on her body. She was in a very serious condi:ion and not fit to appear in court.—The prisoner stated the girl had had a swollen neck for the last six years, and had had some lumps lanced by a doctor in Liverpool Margaret Lancaster, single woman,l3 Peel-street, deposed that he prisoner and his family had occupied her par- lour for ne•rly a fortnight, On Tuesday night about half-past ten the prisoner arrived home and Mrs. Sweeney, when she heard him coining, ran into the kitchen. Sweeney was drunk and when he entered the parlour he asked the girl Ellen, who is 11 years of age where her mother was at the time. She was sitting by the side of the bed which is made on the floor and she replied that her mother had just gone out. The prisoner then struck her on the head and said "You yoaing take your life; I'll make you tell where she is. He after- wards knocked her prostrate on the bed and kicked her, then seizing hold of her throat by both hands, he pressed it until the girls tongue protruded from her mouth. Mrs. Sweeney implored a Mr. Roach , who was in the house to "go to save Ellen before he kills her," and Roach responded by walking into the parlour, and rescued,the girl from her father's violence. The girl in her terror ran out of the house and fell unconscious in the street. Witness and another person carried the girl to Dr. Hutchinson's sucgery. Her neck was red, and the marks of the prisoner's fingers were plainly to be seen, while her upper lip was black.—The pr;soner was remand until next Thurs lay.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST A FARMER'S SON.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE AGAINST A FARMER'S SON.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr J. Brundrit and Mr. C. Reynolds, a young man named Joseph Wilkinson, son of a farmer of Aston Heath Farm, Aston by Sutton, was summoned to answer a charge 8f having on the 23rd September committed a rape upon Ann Bradbury. who was at the time a domestic servant in the employ of Mrs. Dodds. of Aston-lane. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys appeared for the complainant, and Mr. A. Fletcher, of Northwich, for the defendant. After having commenced his opening statement, Mr. Humphreys passed on to the Bench a slip of paper which he said he had just received from Mrs. Bradbury, who, it transpired, said the date ought to be the 30th September, and not the 23rd as slated on the summons.—Mr. Fletcher said the whole case was absurd on the face of it, and he objected to the alteration of the date. Ile was prepared to ,show that the defendant was not near the place on the 23rd , September, and now they wanted to alter the date.—Mr. Humphreys said, if his friend objected, he could ' not wry thrt e.uo further that day. Mr. Fletcher coni- plaincd of Mr. FL um phrey's opening o a a serious charge like this, and then wanting to alter date. Mr. Humphreys replied that the mistake in the date was not his; and heg had only just received intimation of the fact Mr, Fletcher said the object of the summons was not to Fe a committal for rape,—no one would dream of committing a man for such an offence when there was no complaint made for three months. The object was to try and get some evidence which would affiliate the child which was expected to be born. It was unfair to bring a charge of this description against a man in the way this had been brought. Mr. Brundrit said the Bench knew nothing of tho circumstances, but it seemed rather strange that* nothing should have been known before now.—Mr Fletcher liop4d it Would gb forth that there was no slur upon his clietlVB itataaer.—The case wa,s dismissed. WIDNES COUNCIL OF EDUCATION.

The annual meeting of subscribers to this institu- tion, was held in the Lunch Room at Messrs. Haskell, Deacon, and Co.'s Works, yesterday after- noon week. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, J.P., the presi- dent, occupied the chair, and there were also present the Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. Father Cla-k, Jr. S. K. Muspratt, J.P.. Mr. Holbrook Haskell, Jun., J.P., and Mr. IL Wade Deacon, J.P. (hon. sec.). The hon. secretary presented the fifth annual report, which stated :—This has been the second Year during which the present scheme of prizes has been in existence, and the "bronze medals" prizes are awarded for the first time. Below in a tabular form is given the number of children in each school who have gained the rewards
St. Bede's Luke' St. Mary's NatOnal St. Pateck's Sirarn's Cross Warrington-rd. I'Ve.t Dank

303 365 610 572 1790 It is most satisfactory to notice that there has again been a large increase in the number of prize winners. This number hat increased year by year since the foundation of thn Council and there- are now '1,700 prize winners out of 6,370 children on the rolls. When it is remembered that out of these 1,790 children 303 have never missed an attendance for two years, and that 305 have not missed an attendance for one year, there is room for wonder at the regularity of attendance and good health of so many of the children of Widnes. On. the other hand the Council has failed in its efforts to reach .;the very bad attenders. Perhaps no other result could have been expected; for the main cause of the bad attendance of the children is the negligence of the parents, and this negligence the Council is unable to remove. Still the average attendance is hnprovinz, if slowly.. In 1883 when the Council w 53 founded, the average attendance was 75'6 per cent., and last sear it was 84.0 per cent. Hew much of this increase is 'due to the action of the Council, and how much to that of the School Board it is not possible or necessary to determine; but the Council may fairly claim its Pill share. The directors are glad to he able still to report that the majority of the children who wit r bank books are allowed by their parents to retain possession of them. The grants in connection with the two free scholarships at the Farnworth Grammar School were awarded for two rears. The following named gentlemen are thern directors who retire this year by rotation :—Messrs. R. Holden Davies, H. Gaskell, jun., S. K. Muspratt, T. Sutton Thrimis, and J. White. The directors arc pleased to be able to report that since the last annual meeting some fresh members have joined the Council and the subscriptions have consequently increased. The statement of accounts showed that the receipts had reached a total of £240 us. 10d. and the expenditure amounted to £235 2s. 3d., leaving a balance of £5 95. 7d. —The Chairman moved the .adoption of the report, and having been inforrned by the hon. secretary that the Ipercentage of attendance was the highest ever attained in Whines, remarked that the report was eminently satisfactory. The scheme of the Council necessitated theexpenditure of a great deal of money and the manufacturers and inhabitants had subscribed very generously, but the increase in the number of prize winners would cause the income of the Council not to be equal to the expenditure, and a debit balance of about £3O was anticipated for next year. They hoped to obtain this sem either by increased subscriptions or by an addition 'to the number of subscribers. He alluded with gratification to the fact That the inculcation of thrift, one of the principal ideas Alf the council, was meet- ing with great success. The majority of bank accounts that had been opened on behalf of the children were still in existence, and the Council had every reason to be satisfied. (Wear, hear.) Emig' in the new year; a public meeting would be held to decide the scheme upon which the Connell should work in the future .---The report was adopted. On the motion of Dean Finegan, the retiring directors were re-appointed With theaddition of the name of the Rev. G. H. St. Patrick Garrett.—Mr. F. H. Gessage was re-appointed hon. treasurer and Mr. Deacon was re-elected hon. secretary, ' the latter gentle- man being referred to in very flattering terms.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the Board, was held at the Town Mill; on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmis. J.P., presided and then were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Major Wareing, T. Heyes, H. Wade Deacon, P. H. Davies, C. E. Barlow, G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: ItiSTRICT EDUCATICriC COMMITTEE.
div.p: ItiSTRICT EDUCATICriC COMMITTEE.

This Committee reported that during November there were 163 applications for the payment of school fees, which were sre.commended to be paid in 154 cases. 253 persons were summoned before the Committee for contra- vention of the Education Act; 71 were prosecuted before ;the magistrates, 69 were emrrieted.
INCREASES OF SAT.AEY.

The School Mana,gement Ccrai-mittee recommended that the salaries e 30 teachers of the Board Schools, be increased in accordance with the rules of the Board. The aggregate increase was equal to £l4O a year.—The minute was passed.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £4,563 Bs. 5d., of which £3,748 12s. sd. was repayment of loans and interest. The receipts for the month amounted to £1,391 4s. 9d. There was no other business of public interest.

WIDNES WESLEYAN METHODIST CIRCUIT. The quarterly meeting was held at Lacey-street school on Monday. The local preachers met at half past two, the stewards at four o'clock, and a sump- tuous tea was provided at five o'clock by Mr. and Mrs. S. Sadler, of which upwards of 120 officers and friends from all parts of the circuit partook. After tea a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. and Mrs. Sadler on the motion of the stewards (M.essrs. S, Robinson and R. Fogg) supported by. Messrs. B. Brown, R. Webster, and P. Glover. Mr. Sadler responded with a few apt and humourous remarks. The business meeting was held at seven o'clock. The Rev. T. Law presided, and was sup- ported by his colleague Mr. J. Bryant. The finan- cial statement for the quarter, which was submitted by the stewards, was fairly satisfactory, and the report as to the membership—total 632 (increase of 13 on the 'quarter) and 179 juvenile members-- which was submitted by the Rev. T. Law was also satisfactory, and showed that the good done by the Rev. T. Waugh appeared to have the stamp of per- manency upon it. The work at Moss Bank was mak- iugsteady progress, the contributions and the number of members and congregations being on the increase. Mr. Stringer read the account of the worn out ministers' fund, which had likewise' increased considerably ; and the Circuit magazine was reported to be making good progress. The Committee appointed to select a minister in place of the Rev. J. Bryant, who leaves next Con- ference, stated that they had heard several preachers, but they had not yet made a selection. Mr. Robinson was re-appointed circuit chapel secretary ; the circuit stewards were also re-elected; and the leaders of the Matins Hall and Bold mis- sions reported that both were being largely attended.

div.head: RUNCOAN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCOAN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The ordinary meeting of the above-named Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse. on Thursday, when there were present—Colonel Ashton (in the chair), the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. E. Mclntyre, E. Aaron, J. Stokes, Lewis, Parr, Baguley, Brandreth, 11. Linaker (clerk), .T. Farrington (inspector of nuisances).

div.head: A- SURCHA RGE REMITTED.
div.p: A- SURCHA RGE REMITTED.
A letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that a surcharge of £65 4s. 7d., made in 1887 on, Colonel Ashton, had been remitted. The surcharge was in reference to the Appleton sewerage.
ARRANGEMENi FOR CASES OF INFECTION.

A letter was read from the Town Clerk of Warrington enquiring about the population of the district over which the Authority proposed to arrange for the use of the Warrington infectious diseases hospital. It was decided, on the motion of Mr. Brasidreth, seconded by Mr. Aaron, that the Clerk be instructed to ascertain the population of Appleton, Higher and Lower Walton, Hatton and Stretton, and report to the Town Clerk of Warrington.

div.head: FRODSH.A.II RATES..
div.p: THE FRODSH.A.II RATES..

It was reported that a summons had been issued against the overseers of Frodshatn for the balance of special sanitary rate. It was decided that the summons should be adjourned until the assistant-overseer had been appointed.—The Assistant Clerk informed the Board that the sum sued for was £lBO, and that £750 would be required on special sanitary rate and poor rate before the 25th March next.—Mr. Davies (the overseer) appeared before the Authority, and asked the Board to adjourn the summons until the appointment of assistant overseer had been made.—Mr. Brandreth said that one gentleman had told him that he had lived at Frodsham twelve mouths, and had never been asked for the payment ef a poor rate or for gas.—Some discussion then ensued as to paying of the present collector, after which it was decided to adjourn the summons for three weeks, the overseers to pay the expenses connected with the adjournment.

div.head: ALLEGRO JERRY-BUILT PROPERTY.
div.p: ALLEGRO JERRY-BUILT PROPERTY.

Mr. Parr said he had been asked by two persons to make an inquiry respecting the erection of property in the neighbourhood of Warrington. So far as lie knew, cottage property, when being built in Warrington, was inspected by the Sanitary Inspector and if it was not built according to the rules of the Authority, he under- stood that complaints were made about it. The only question was whe her the districts outside Warrington came under the same laws as Warrington.—The Clerk replied in the negative, and said that the matter was discussed about the building bye-laws some years ago' - but nothing had yet boon definitely settled.—The subject then dropped.
NEINV HOUSES AT lIELSBY AND. APPLETON.

An application was made on behalf of Messrs. Guest and Son for a certificate of occupation for certain houses - erected by them at He!shy ; but - owing to the intended wath supply to the same not being satisfactory, the. application was refused. A certificate of occupation was r ranted to Mr. T. 11. Lyon for a new house erected by him at Appleton, the water supply being satisfac- tory. This was the whole of the business. THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY " ARIBL."

That although the subject of Baths appertrs to have been lost eight of at present, it has not been forgotten and the Committee that has charge of the matter, held a meeting this week. That up to within a few weeks ago, it was the rule of the Runcorn Bench to impose a fine of ss. and costs upon each delinquent charged wii,h r drunkenness. On two consecutive Mondays, fines as low as 2s. GI and costs have been inflicted, and many people are wondering what is the cause of this leniency. That no fault is found with this new acptur as each case should be judged on its merits. That Mr. Bob Sawyer in Pickwick had a unique and diverting way of making known the firm of "Sawyer late Norkemorf," but our local "Sawbones," Stl2ll Weller would have styled the medical men of Runcorn, appear to be able to keep themselves before the public without recourse to that young gentleman s lively methods. That having regard to surgery hours, and the exacting nature of a physician's profession, one does not expect him to be punctual in -his amuse- ments; but, there, was a mirth-Provoking unani- mity about the way in which the doctor' turned. up at the Tonic Sol-Fa concert on Monday? That half an hour after the concert had sturted, live medical men entered the room close upon each others heels, and passed before the platform in full 'iew of the audience, and a broad smile overspread more than one face at the strange coincidence. That they were a handsome-looking lot. That all that was needed to make the coneert a grand success Was a larger audience. ,That much satisfaction is expressed in Widn'es at-the selection of Mr. E. li. Muspratt as candidate for the County Council, and it is thought highly improbable that he will be opposed.

RUGBY.

Ilaurosi v. Rtrricoax Rzcmi,los 2an —Played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and resulted : Halton, one goal and five minors ; Recreation, one goal and two minors. STAR RECREATION V. RUNCORN VICTORIA.—PIayed OR the ground of the former on Saturday, and ended in a win for the visitors: Runcorn Victoria, one try, six minors ' • Star Recreation, nil. ST. HELENS WASPS V. Drrrox Rac's.—This match was played at Gerard's Bridge on Saturday. When the whistle sounded for time the score was—Wasps, two tries, eleven minors; Roe's nil. RUNCORN Tatra Bram V. RUNCORN Rovirits.—A very pleasant match was played on the former's ground, on 'Saturday. The final score stood—Blues, 3 tries and 8 minors ; Rovers, 1 try and 4 minors. ORFORD RANGERS v. WARRINGTON JITNIORS.—This match was played on the pound of the former on Satur- day, and res,lted in a win for the visitors by 8 tries, .7 minors, to 2 minors. Hayes, Booth, and Plinston played a gucycl game forth. rumors. FRODSHAM RECREATION V. WESTON.—This match was played on the ground of the former, and Weston-won by, one goal, one try, four minors, to one try and two minors. Hulse and Pendlebury gained tries for Weston, Mort kicking a goal. The try for Frodsham was obtained by J. Goodall. Ruaicoax v. LIVERPOOL OLD BOYS (Second Teams).— The match arranged between these teams was played on Saturday. at Fairfield. Runcorn startedge play at 3.30. At half-time the game was—Old Boys 2 Onors, Runcorn I minor. Final result: Runcorn A, 1 goal, 2 tries, 5 minors, Old Boys 2 minors. • RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH V. WIDNES VEST BANK RAI:GRAIL—This match was played on the ground of the Church in dull weather. A good but uninteresting game ended in a draw and slightly in favour of the Church, who scored 1 try 4 minors to 1 try. Peacock scored for, the Church and Jackson for the Rangers. WIDNES "A" v. ST. HELENS "A."—This match was contested at Widnes, before a moderate number of spectators. "Two twenties" were played. Widnes kick- ing off. Several minors were scored in quick succession, following which Holt obtained a beautiful try, but the place kick was a failure. Hardman next got over and scored another try, which was converted into a goal by Johnson. The visitors afterwards got' a drop goal. Final result—Widnes 1 goal, 1 try, 4 minors ; St. Helens, 1 goal (dropped.) WIDNES V. ST. HELENS.—These Rugby teams met on the ground of the latter, before thousands of spectators on Saturday St. Helens kicked off: Allen failed at a free kick, a minor resulting to the home team. Clark obtained a try, which he failed to improve, and a minor followed. Smith immediately obtained another try for Widnes, which Plumpton converted into a goal, Score at half-time :—Widnes 1 goal 1 try 2 minors, St. Helens 2 minors. In the second half the play was exceedingly even, the ball travelling from one end of the field to the other in rapid succession. Towards the close of the game a thick mist came on and the players could not be distinguished. Final result :—Widnes 1 goal 1 try 2 minors. St. Helens 2 minors. WARRINGTON" A" V. MANCHESTER ATHLETIC IST.— At Manchester. At the time of starting the field was onveloped in a dense fog, so dense that the pldyers, 20 yaras away, could hardly be discerned. It was first arranged by the captains to play two 15 minutes, and the result to be declared a draw. The game had been in progress about 20 minutes under these conditions when the fog suddenly lifted, and at once it was decided to restart, and play the proper game, Holmes, who had been hurt during the early game, being deputed to play three-quarter. Two ten minutes having been agreed, Warburton commenced hostilities with a long kick, but Fox taking the ball cleverly replied with a run. A rush by the Warringtonians, however, headed by Beard, Hayes, and Ashurst, took the ball back. From a pack near the quarter flag Mather, after feigning to pass, dashed through the scrimmage, but a throw forward spoiled the chance. A dodgy run and kick by Lillias removed the scene of action to half way, but sharp passing between Hayes and Molyneaux and a strong rush by the latter brought the ball back. Bate Adamson, and Ratcliffe were now conspicuous by good passing, and from a scrim- mage at the Athletic quarter flag Mather passed to Speakman, who threw to Bibby, and after a splendid dodgy run he dashed across the line, gaining the first try, Warburton placing a goal. The home team, evidently nettled by this reverse, quickly kicked off, the ball being ruled back for off-side. Some very pretty passing by Williams, Mather, Holmes, and Daniels, and a fine run by the latter, were the next items, Cope relieving temporarily by a good kick. Half-time was called with Warrington a goal a-head. Fox lost rico time in re-startma., the ball being well . . .

- returned to centre. From the 'line-out Warrington, headed by Warburton, Molvneaux. and Ashurst, deibbled down the field, Lillias saving. Some good play by Rigby, who was now playing forward, was evidently relished by the spectators, but Jolley replied with a good kick to centre. Fine running and passing' by Mather, Holmes, Speakman, and Bibby again caused the home team to be pressed. From a line-out Warbur- ton secured, and giving Speakman a splendid pass, he dodged several opponent and dropped an unmistakable goal. Fox kicked off, Warburton replying with a good kick, and good following up found Stretton tackled with the ball. Scrambling play was now indulged in, neither side claiming advantage. Warrington at length had ' another look in, and Lillias mulling the ball, Bate ha4po difficulty in grounding between the posts, the place kick failing. The drop-out found Fox to the fore with some good play, and Harper joining him play was taken to half way. Daniels returned, but dribbling by Wade, Lillias, awl Stretton saw the ball lodged in mid- field. Jolley was next prominent with a fine punt, and Mather taking up the running had hard lines in not scoring, the ball being kicked dead. The drop-out was mulled, which enabled the home team to reach Warring- ton territory. From a loose dribble Daniels picked up, and making a magnificent run was only stopped on the goal-line. Hartley, Rigby. and Wade dribbled out of danger, when some beautiful passing between Williams, Holmes, Speakman, and Daniels only resulted in a minor, time being called with the score—Warrington 2 goals, 1 try. 2 minors to nil. The combination of Wamogton was perfect 4 the passing of the whole team being quite a treat. The Athletic was best represented by Fox. Lillias, and Wade. Teams :—Warrington "A" : Back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Daniels, Speakman, and Bibby ; half-backs, Mather and Williams • forwards, Molyneaux, Hayes, Ashurst, Holmes, Beard, Ratcliffe, Bate, Warburton, and Adamson. Athletic: Back, Rigby; three-quarter backs, Stretton, Cope, and Fox • half- backs, Harper and Lillias; forwards, Neary, Hartley, Wade, Williams, Romans, Burke, Brown, and

RUNCORN v. LIVERPOOL OLD 1301 R—This important fixture, which has been looked forward to with much I interest, was played off on Saturday on the Irwell-lane I ground, Runcorn, in the presence of an enthusiastic 1 and large number of spectators, who were drawn to the , field in the expectation of witnessing an exceptionally good game. Nor were they in any way disappointed as the teams of both clubs were about the strongest that could be selected on either side, and the play was of a most meritorious and pleasing character. It is always a treat to witnegg a game contested in a most friendly manner, and yet fought out with that energy and vigour which is clear evidence that the contestants, on behalf of their respective teams are determined to yield no point which would endanger their success. This was the spirit in which play proceeded between the clubs under notice. The teams, as will be seen from the list, were strong, and were for Runcorn : Brazendale, back; W. A. Riley, G. T. Wainwright, and T. Woods, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and W. Evans, half backs; W. H. Broady, W. Elu,ghes, R. Dolan, F. Han- cock, W. Faulkner, W. Rigby, P. Riley, J. Gayter, and W. Stubbs, forwards. For the Old Boys the selection was as follows :—F. Hiekson, back: W. Legge, A. E. Ash, and F. Atkinson, three-quarter backs ; H. D. Woods and J. B. O'Dwyer, half backs; Dr. Chapman, F Chambers, J. A. Brodie, E. W. Bullen, R. Goold, J. C. Goold, H. It. Townsend, W. E. Edmunds, and J. Hen- shaw, forwards. W. Hughes kicked off at the time appointed. Woods' return being charged, the ball watt into touch. Brazendale and Woods then exhibited good form,and the home forwards,who were led byGayterand Faulkner, gave a capital example of following up, with the result that Hickson was cempelled to put in a saving clause. Runcorn then pressed their opponents in a vigorous manner, and play was confined for some time near the visitors line. F. Chambers, however, dribbled in
KAY'S COMPOUND Essence of Linseed, Aniseed, Senegn, Squill, Tolu, &c., with Chlorodyne, 9d, 13L, &c. Ada.

fine style, and thus relief was temporarily given. Some excellent kicking was then observed on the part of Wain- wright and Ash for their respective sides, and Brazendale gave clear evidence that he was determined to register a goal on behalf of the Runcernians. He took a kick at goal from a place, but to the regret of the local spectators, only a minor was the result. The forwards then engaged ' in some arduous work, and Brazendale again put in one of his long kicks. The ball landed. near Hickson, who, however, mulled. H. Hughes watched his oppor- tunity, followed up, and was within an ace of scoring. Ash came to the rescue, and the Liverpool 25 was the scene of a warm contest. W Legge, who was in the act ' of making a dodgy run, was splendidly collared by Riley. The home captain was well to the front, and Wainwright, who obtained possession of the sphere, ran up with much dash, and was only collared in the nick of time. The visitor's wereagain pressed, and W. Evans got over, and secured a try. The kick at goal was reserved to Woods, but the essay was attended wit.la failure. The game then became very fast, and shortly after the drop out, Hickson pat in a splendid kick, thereby relieving. The ball was worked by degrees up to the home citadel by the visitors' forwards; but Brazendale, ever on the alert, was called upon to relieve. After putting in a capital run he punted the ball to the Liverpool 25. Danger, how- ever, was averted by Legge, who ran and kicked well. This brought up half-time, with the score for the home team 1 try 3 minors, and no register for the visitors. The Old Boys, on the resumption of play, showed a thorough determination to equalize matters, and the energy anii good play of the men of Runcorn had only one apparent object, that being to put them on the metal. Chapman kicked off, but the Old Boys were soon under the necessity to save owing to the combined play of Runcorn. For Runcorn, Stubbe gained decided prominence for the dash with which he played. Ash greatly aided the visitors by his judicious play, but a good chance was missed by Legge, who let go the ball. Townsend dribbled with remarkable ability, and the ball was taken well into the territory of the home team. Brazendale rescued, and picked up smartly, and by an excellent rush; placed the play in the Old Boy's quarters. At this point of the game the play was fast and furious, and the greatest excitement prevailed, the scene of hostilities being the territory of the visitors, who were compelled to play a defensive game. Passing of an excwitionally high order was indulged in by Evans, Wainwright, and Hughes, which aided the home team most materially. The tackling of Brazendale was superb. H. Hughes scored from a scrimmage on the line, but again there was a failure in converting. Ash, too, had a drop at eoal credited him, but the ball struck the posts, and bounded out. Runcorn then touched down. The game,after perhaps the most exciting play that has been witnessed on the Run- corn ground, ended in a victory for the wearers of the myrtle green by 2 tries and 4 minors, to 2 minors scored by the Old Boys.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. MOSELEY.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. MOSELEY.

The last-named organisation opened their Lancashire tour on Saturday, when they opposed the Warrington- ians at their spacious enclosure at Wilderspool. It will be remembered that eur local team first encountered the premier Birmingham club when on a short tour last season, and though the ",wirepullers " succeeded in lowering the Moseleyi es' colours, they could not refer to the match with pleasure, when it is taken into account that the majority of the team were more or less crippled during the encounter. This fact coupled with the miserable state of the atmosphere, no doubt accounted ,for the moderate attendance, and when the visitors set the oval in motion there would probably be only 2,500 people present. Antrobu.s was an absentee on the Warrington side, whilst it was pleasing to note that Jolley made his re-appearance in the team. The visitors mustered their best fifteen. Off-side play from the kick-off ruled a pack at midfield, and the first to make headway was Barnes, who ran to the Moseley quarter flag. Rogers and Nicholls dribbled well, and a smart save by Massey met with due appre- ciation. The Warringtonians by a combined rush, took the game back to the Moseley lines, where Mylius was called upon to defend. Jolley stopped a movement here in accurate style, and an effort by Fair. Turner from a line-out was nipped in thebud by Mason tackling him just on the verge of scoring. A minor followed to the homesters' credit. Froni the drop-out Fair. Turner made his mark, punt- ing into touch close to the Moseley line. Quick passing by the Warrington backs almost brought about the downfall of the Moseley goal, for a shot by Barnes had the misfortune to strike the post in transit. The ball rebounded into play, and Barnes and Massey in turn both threatened danger. A weak pass served as a relief to Moseley, until exchange kicks by Frank Turner and Mylius ended with advantage to the Warringtonians. Evans was now for the first time called on to defend his charge, which he did with credit. Another chance was- missed by the Warringtonians, until a grand pass from Barnes to Massey gave the latter an opportunity, which only resulted in a minor' the shot at goal missing by the nearest shade. Hard luck was experienced by the home division soon after the drop-out, and time aftertime glaring opportunities of scoring were missed. Jolley exchanged kicks with Smith, and Oswald was the means if tennporary relief being brought to his side. The visitors now showed up, and mulling by the Warrington backs allowed the Moseleyites to rush up, and A. Smith had the satisfaction of securing the win- ning point of the match. No goal resulted from the place kick. ' Warrington now showed up with extra exertions, but Rogers forced Massey to kick dead, after he had dribbled accurately. A misfortune • unfortu- nately here befel the Warringtonians, for Massey in tackling Smith met with serious injuries, which neces- sitated his immediate retirement. Notwithstanding this piece of ill-luck, the Warringtonians were not dis- couraged, and a grand run by Jolley almost had the desired effect. Half-time was called with the score— Moseley, one try, one minor; Warrington, two minors. During the second half the ground was enveloped in a dense fog, in fact, the players could not be distinguished more thad a few yards away. It is impossible to give a detailed report of the latter portion of the game, but from what could be gleaned through the mist, the Warringtonians were in an aggressive atti ude the greater portion of the game. Rough play was the chief order, and a sad occurrence which undoubtedly blemished the Moseley team victory, was the suspension i of Rogers from participating further in the match. ' Nevins was executing some work when, without the least provocation,tßogers struck him in the face. Upon appeal to Mr. Lord, Rogers was rightly ordered from the field of play. Returning to the match, Warrington still pressed, and minors were ' quickly added, but despite extra efforts, the •• wirepullers" could not gain a major point, and in the end Moseley retired victors by one try, one minor, to five minors. Teams :—Warring- ton Evans, back ; Jolley, Barnes, and Massey, three- quarter backs; Speakman and Lawless, half backs; Ashton, Fair Turner, W. Povey, Littlewood, Nevins, F. Turner, Unsworth, Randles, and Dillon, forwards. Moseley: Oswald, back; Albert, Smith, Mylius, and Mason, three-quarter backs; A. Palethorpe and Rogers half back ;H. Rogers, Nicholl, Lycett, E. R. Lycett, R. Palethorpe, Lean, Dawes, and Jackson, forwards. Referee, Mr. Lord, Broughton.

div.head: WORKMEN:
div.p: WORKMEN:
MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AND HIS

The London' Star" thus answers some accusa- tions made against Mr. Brunner, ALP., by the Lon- don "Evening News." What, then, are the facts of this case? In the first place, Mr. Brunner has nothing whatever to do with the management of the department in which the alleged grievances took place. Be is concerned with the financial, and the finanCial part alone, of his firm. He has never employed, he has never dismissed, one solitary man in the works. This is a statement which probably he would be too proud to make on his own behalf • we make it on our own responsibility, and with full know- ledge of the farts. But we do not want to rest the acquittal we shall demand for Mr. Brunner on this plea, the insufficiency of which we are quite ready to acknow- ledge. We ask whether the firm can, be held guilty of being oppressive to its workmenin face of the following incontestable facts.

Mr. Brunner is the member for the division in which his works are situated. He had a splendid majority both in 1885, when he was first elected ; and in 1887 when he was re-elected. In the one case it was 1,028 ; in the other, it was 1,129. But these majorities, how- ever large, might have beat turned into a minority if his own workmen, or even a portion of them, had •oted against him. There are in the works no less than 2,000 men ; most of them are entitled to the franchise; and it is, therefore, plain to any understanding that if the employes of Mr. Brunner wished to defeat him they could have done so; and Mr. 13runner has always abstained from any act which could in the least inter- fere with the perfect freedom of choice on the part of his men: He has never canvassed or allowed canvass- ing among his men. Indeed at the laSt election some- body had placed upon the 'factory walls an appeal in favour of Lord Henry Grosvenor, the Unionist candi- date, and Mr. Brunner refused to allow it to be taken down.

There are many other pro'ofs of the esteem and affec- tion in which Mr. Brunner is held by those workmen whom he is falsely represented as oppressing. He has twice had to go on long vacations for the benefit of his health. When he returned home in 1883 this tyrant was welcomed by the whole town. The horsed were taken from his carriage ; and he was led in triumph to his home. Again, in 1887, when he returned after an absence, the whole town was ablaze with bunting, his own workmen came to the station to receive him; and he was presented with an address of hearty and affec- tionate welcome.

. • The firm are charged (1) with overworking their men; (2) with dismissing them capriciously (3) with giving:them unhealthy employment; (4) with giving them small wages; and (5) with general neglect of their duties as employers, Let us take these charges in suc- cession.

Firsr, as to overwork. It is quite true that the works are employed continuously. It was proposed by the firm itself some time ago that the work should be sus- pended for a portion of Sunday; the men themselves protested against the proposal, and it was abandoned in obedience to their representations. , Second, as to capricious dismissal; this charge is dis- proved by the fact that nearly every single one of the men that were 'employed by the firm in UM when it first started, are still in the employ of the firm. Third, as to the employment being unhealthy, this is disproved by one single fact. The house of Mr. Mold and the house of Mr. Brunner—the two principal part- ners in the firm—are at the. works. Mr. Brunner has a large family; and a sturdier and healthier family there is not in all Cheshire_ The place cannot be very unhealthy when Mr. Brunner is willing to keep his-own wife and children at the nearest spot to the works at which a house could be erected.

Fourth, as to the charge of the wages 6eing too low. The works are conducted entirely under Trade Union Rules. Ws don't believe there is a man in the works who is not a trade Unionist. We shall be somewhat surprised to find that the local Union is not as well able t's take care of the interests of its members as a gentle- man who calls himself a Socialist, and is really a Tory agent ; or a newspaper which represents the Tory party. And, finally, as to the general charge of neglect of duty as employers of labour we' have to call attention to these facts. Close to the works the firm have built cottages, comfortable, clear, and healthy, for 150 of their workmen ; and that the rents are sufficiently moderate is proved by the fact that for their outlay upon these cottages the firm receive exactly 3 per cent. The firm have built and endowed schools; they subscribe largely to the cricket club which the workmen have established; Mr Brunner erected a library at an expense of £5,000 in the town of Northwich, and the firm volun- tarily tax themselves for the rate so as to give their workmen the advantage of the library gratuitously. We doubt, indeed, if there be any body of workmen in the kingdom who are happier or better situated than the men who have the advantage of working for Mr. Brunner and his firm.

Of his own private benefactions, perhaps it is not necessary to speak. We could mention half a dozen institutions for the benefit of the masses to which he is a constant and a regular subscriber. But we do think it our duty to reveal to the public the fact that within the last two years Mr. Brunner "has placed £l,OOO at the dis- posal of the leaders of the Irish movement to be expended in defence of the Irish tenantry. When a man who has done so much for his fellow man is attacked, one may well despair of the utility of using one's position generously. It would seem that it is safer to be a Tory sweater than to be a generous, considerate, and humane Radical employer.

div.head: CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c.
div.p: CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c.

Messrs. George Bell' and Sons, Covent Garden, London, the publishers of Bohn's Standard Works, are issuing a popular edition of Captain Marryat's tales. We have received two volumes of this series—" Peter Simple" 'and "Mr. Midshipman Easy." They are well-printed on good paper, and are handsomely bound in blue and gold ; price 3s. 6d. each. There are, eight full-page illustrations to each story; and they 'are all admirably executed. The illustrations of "Peter Simple" are by Mr. F. A. Fraser, and thoseo "Mr. Midshipman Easy" by Mr. E. J. Wheeler. It is not necessary now-a- days to commend Captain Marryat's stories ; they have commended themselves for a generation. They are full of stirring adventure, lively wit, and good, sense, and the boy who has yet to read them has a fine treat in store for him. As a Christmas present, there are few things that would give greater pleasure to a boy than a copy of either "Peter Simple "or" Mr. Midshipman Easy." The December issue of the Catnelot series, published by Mr. Walter Scott, is a volume of essays on dm English poets, by Mr. James Russell Lowell. It is a matter of course to say that whatever Mr. Lowell writes is well worth reading, 1-4 pt the learned and clever American has seldom written anything more readable than these essays. The thought is weighty, without giving the impression of heaviness, for it ip al*a.ys expressed with epigrammatic point and clearness. The subjects of the essays are :—Spencer, Shakespeare, Milton, Words- worth, Keats, Lessing, and Rosseau, and the Sentimenta- lists.

In the Canterbury Poets, from the same firm, we have Milton's Paradise Regained," and the poet's minor poems. The volume is edited by Dr. Bradshaw, M.A., Inspector of Schools, Madras, and the reader may therefore confidently rely on the accuracy of the text. We must confess to a partiality for this dainty edition of the poets, and this latest on Milton fully equals its predecessors, _ _ _

"The Bairns' Annual" (Messrs. Field and Tuer, London) is a shilling volume of old-fashioned Fairy Tales, Sm., edited by Alice Corkran. The book is illtistrated with about 100 wood blocks and a coloured frontispiece, and its object is to give fairy tales in their original form. To this end, the illustrations are as old-fashioned as the text. To the grandmother, it will be in the nature of a revival, and to the child a surprise. "People we Meet," is a series of full-page illustra- tions by Mr. Harry Parkes, the text, which is the minor thing in this instance, being supplied by Mr. Charles Rideal. These character sketches are 24 in number, and they are instinct with life--everyone of them. The issue is "a palpable hit;" and it ought to have a great

The Crofters' Commission issued on Wednesday their first decision on Lady Matheson's property in the island of Lewis. They have granted an average reduction of 42 per cent, on the rents of 150 crofter tenants in the parish of Barvas, and of total arrears amounting to £2,422 they have cancelled £2,043.

A num4r of evictions were carried out on Wednesday on the property of Mr. W. Lloyd, Tower Hill, Cappa- more, county Limerick. Seven tenants, their families, and effects were turned into the roadway, but there was no resistance to the bailiffs and police, except in the (wges of three tenants, who barricaded their doors.

div.head: 11C.AAHNER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 22, 1888.
div.p: 11C.AAHNER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 22, 1888.

run- "People we meet" will be preserved by those who purchase a copy. "Men, Maidens and Manners a Hundred years ago" is also published by Messrs. Field and Tuer, and it is quite a novelty in its way. It is a record, as the title suggests,of the life from month to month that our great- grandfathers and great-grandmothers lived. It is from the pen of Mr. John Ashton, who his done his work judiciously ; but the contemporary illustrations—thirty- four ia number—are the chief feature. The following ; singular paragraph will interest our Lancashire readers— "Thismonth (Feb. 1787) there occurred a very singu- lar case of contagious hysteria, which is well worth Inoting. On February 15, at a eetton manufactory at Hodder bridge, in Lancashire, a girl put a mouse into the breast of another girl, who had a great dread ef mice. The girl immediately was seized with violent convulsions, which lazted twenty-four hours. On the following day, three more girls were similarly seized ; on the 17th, six more. This created great alarm, and the mill was stopped. as it was thought that these strange attacks might possibly be owing to something in the cotton. On the 18th, three; and on the 19th, eleven more were attacked by thisstrange malady, making in all twenty-four cases. Of these twenty-one were young women, two girls, and one man. The symptons were— anxiety, a feeling of strangulation, and very strong con- vulsions, which were so violent as to last, without intermission, from a quarter of an hour to twenty-four hours, and to require the assistance of four or five per- sons to prevent the patients from tearing their hair and dashing their heads against the floor or walls. A doctor from Preston cured them by means of electric shocks; and on the 20th:they were sufficiently recovered to have a dance, and the next day all but two or three were at work."

The Christmas Number of " Truth " is in verse as usual, and very bright verse much of it is—hitting off successfully, as it does, the political follies of the day. The main idea is a caricature of the Parnell Commis- sion; and there is some plain-speaking to sundry prominent persons whose doings are not above sus- picion. There are four coloured full-page illustrations, and a score or so of plain ones. Some of them are very comical, and Mr. Chamberlain comes in, as might be expected, for many more kicks than halfpence. "Popular Poets of the Period" is the title of a new publication, price sixpence, which deserves support. It is issued by Messrs. Griffith. Farren and Co. The object is to give "a series of brief biographies of poets of our own time and country, with Interesting specimens of their work." The authors dealt with in the fourth number to hand are :—Professor Blackie, Austin Dobson, Sarah Doudney, Dr. Japp, and William Allinc.fham. From Messrs. Rildesheimer and Faulkner, London, we have received a number of Christmas booklets and Christmas cards which may be pronounced as the high- water mark of art in this direction. This firm spends an enormous sum year by year in securing novel and afri beautiful designs, d every year is an Indication of progress. Amongst the booklets, we have "The Good Shepherd," a poem from the fertile brain of Mr. F. E. Weatherly. It is vigorously illustrated by Alice Reeve, and finely printed in monotint. Sheridan's rellicking song—" Here's to the Maiden of Bashful Fifteen" is jointly illustrated by two such eminent hands as Alice Havers and Ernest Wilson. The figures are finely drawn, and the colouring is delicate and harmonious. Mr. Wilson also illustrates "The Harvest Moon "—a series of selections from Longfellow and other poets. "River Flowers" is illustrated by Mr. Charles G. Noakes who haa-a good eye for such combinations, and it is as it should be, in colours. "The Little Lovers, or aAhousand years ago" is another piece of verse by Mr. F. E. Weatherley, while the illustrations—capital in their way—are by Harriet M. Bennett. Coming to the cards, the variety is so great as to be almost bewildering. Here we have an imitation shell, with a painting of a group of boats on the sea coast, i and here again s a series with the cross for a basis, and beautiful vignettes in the centre. In another set of cprcli we have charmingly executed country cottages; whih in ethers dogs and birds, and flowers are made to do duty in the ,most picturesque way. In one case what seems to be an owl opens out and we have, "Christmas greetings to an owl'd 'friend." Amongst the newest and prettiest designs are medallions of couples at the dance in last century costume. The work is in every respect delicate and finished, and we cannot but think these cards will be in great demand. But all the cards or books issued by Messrs. Hildesheimer and Faulkner are good specimens, so that the purckaser would not go wrong if he made a cheice with his oyes closed. They are worlss of art in miniature.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
-- HOUSE OF COMMONS, MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock.

QuamoNs.—Lord RANDOLPH Cannot= asked sane further questions about the expedition to Suakim, and elicited from Sir Jexas FERGUSSON the information that Lord SALISBURY'S advice to the Egyptian Government to "abandon Suakim at once" was "a statement in which the PRIME MINISTER expressed his own opinion." Sir JAMES declined to say whether it expressed the opinion of Her Mantsry's Government. SUPPLY.—THE SOUDAN.—On the House going into Committee of Supply en the Civil Service Estimates, Mr. Joins Monty raised the question of British policy with regard to the Soudan on a vote for embassies and missions abroad. He complained that Colonel Krrcionaß had irritated and exasperated the coast tribes, and led up to the bringing of the Nile dervishes to the intrenchments in front of Suakin). We ought to pro- claim that Egyptian dominion was not to be extended elle' inch beyond Suakirn in any circumstance whatever. Sir JAMES FEROUSSON said it was quite possible that Osman Digma's letter was only a clever Oriental device. The present Government had simply held the position taken up by the late Government—that Wady Haifa and ISuakim alone should be held. Mr. GLADSTONE said he thought there was still an opportunity for negotiations and that they ought to be attempted by the Government, He for one agreed with Lord Salisbury that there was. ' no Egyptian interest involved in the retention of Suakim After Mr. SrstrEcnni had defended the course which had been adopted, Lord ReNnorrE CHaßcairr made a strong attack on the Government. Mr. MORLEY, in order te take the sense of the House on the Government's action in regard to Suakim, moved a reduction in the I vote, but on a division the motion was rejected by 165 votes to 76. The vote was further assailed by Mr. LABOUCHERE •in order to draw attention to Lord SALISBURY'S recent remarks about "the SAUKVILLE incident," and subsequently there was a discussion on affairs in the region of Lake Nyassa. HOUSE OF LORDS, TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. MISCELLANHOVS.—The Public Health Act Amendment (Buildings in Streets) Bill was read a third time and passed. The Earl of BUNRAYEN, in moving the second reading of the Preferential Payment of Wages (No. 2) Bill, explained that its object was to give the payment of wages in this country the priority they had in other countries in case of bankruptcy or liquidation. The Local Government (England and Wales) Electors Act Repeal Bill, the second reading of which was moved by Lord DENMAN, was rejected without discussion. TEE LIBEL BILL.—The Commons' amendments to the Lords' amendment to the Law of Libel Act Amendment Bill were fixed for consideration on Friday next. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes past five o'clock, until Thursday.

_ _ . HOUSE OF COMMONS, TUBSDAY, The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS.—"CIZEWE AND SANDISAM—MY. AULAREN called attention to an alleged violation by the Lon- don and North-western Railway Company, at Crewe, of a 'section of the Truck Act, which, relates to the appointment of auditors for the pro- tection of the interests of workmen in the company's employment. The. Home Secretary, in reply, stated that the company did not admit that their system constituted a violation of the Act, but he had directed the opinion of the law officers of the Crown to be taken on the point. The Home Secretary, in reply to a question of Mr. Conybeare, put for him by Mr. Sexton, explained that, in the case of the removal of a boy 14 years of age from prison to a reformatory at Sandbach, a handcuff was'used because the warder in charge of the lad was an old and not very active man, and there was reason to apprehend an attempt to frescape. Sir George Campbell gave notice of his intention, next session, to move a resolution affirming that the British Constitution requires amendment. . SUPPLY, Sze.—The House afterwards went into Com- mittee of Supply, resuming with the further considera- tion of the Irish estimates, and several votes were agreed to. The Statute Law Revision (No. 2) Bill passed through committee. The Lords' amendments to the Libel Law Amendment Bill were considered, and, some of them being accepted, a committee was appointed to draw up reasons for disagreeing with the Lords.
The House adjourned at five minutes past four o'clock.
_HOUSE .OF COMMONS, WEDNESDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve.

QLJESTIONS.—In reply to a question by Mr. HANDEL COSSHAM as to whether the Local Government Act con- tained any provision to prevent active partisans of candidates at a county council eleCtion being eligible for the post of presiding officer, Mr. RITCHIE replied that the provisions of the Municipal Corporations Act applied to such elections. By that Act it was provided that no. person should be appointed by the returning officer for the purpose of the election who has been employed by any other person in of about the election. MiscaLrAisootts:-=Lord Brooke, the newly-elected member for Colchester, who was accompained to the table by Mr. Akers-Douglas and Major Rasch, took his seat amidst cheers from the Ministerial benches. The suspension of the standing orders having been agreed to without discussion, report of Supply was proceeded with. Considerablediscussiontook place on different Irish votes, but eventually the work of Supply was completed. The Solicitors Bill passed through Committee. The Suff- ragans Nomination Bill passed !through Committee, and was read a third time and passed. The Liability of Trustees Bill was considered on report, agreed to with the omission of clause 9, read a third time, and passed. The House was counted out at twenty minutes past eight o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS, THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after four o'clock.

MISCELLANEOUS.—The House sap for about an hour. Lord HAnms, replying to the Earl of DUNA/17EN, explained the reasons for the disarmament of the Honourable Artillery Company. Certain rules of the House having been suspended, a number of bills were advanced towards the final stage. The Select Committee on the Sweating System were empowered to employ an inspector to visit various parts of the kingdom under inquiry. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes past five o'clock.
HOUSE OF COMMQNS,, THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three &clock.

QUESTIONS.—MT. PLUNKET informed Colonel BLDNDELL that the 25in. Ordnance map of Lanca.shire would, it was hoped, be completed in four years. Mr. STANHOPE said the Royal warrant of the Honourable Artillery Company had not been withdrawn, nor would such a step be taken without very careful inquiry. Owing to the-existing state of discipline the cores could not be recognised as efficient, and the usual course had been adopted of withdrawing the arms ; but he hoped that beim e long a reorganisation of the corps would take place which would put it in a satisfactory condition. Mr. H. B. REED questioned the HOME SECRETARY about a report that threats had been used at certain Yorkshire markets towards per- sons dealing with distrained cattle from Ireland. Mr. Marrnews said there was some evidence to show that there had been attempts to interfere by threats with till sale of cattle at Leeds, Halifax, and Wakefield, and if he could procure sufficient evidence he should direct pmsecutions to be instituted. The right hon. gentleman added that he had no evidence to show that there was any indisposition on the part of purchasers to buy. ItAINEILL ASYLIIM.—Mr. RITCHIE was questioned about the proposed'pensning of the medical officer of the Rainhill Asylum and, after stating the law, said the Local Government ,S.l Gard had no jurisdiction in the matter.

THE Barrus AT SUAICIM.—After Mr. Stanhope had read, amidst cheers, General Greenfell's report of the engagement at Suakim, Sir James Fergusson said instructions had been sent to Her Majesty's Consul General at Zanzibar to warn the Sultan of the disastrous consequences to himself likely to ensue from the course he had just entered upon. On the motion for the second reading of the Appropriation Bill various hon. members brought forward grievances which had previously during the present session been Wire or less under discussion, and a short debate tool place on the Suakiin expeditiom and British policy in Egypt. The second reading was agreed to, and the House adjourned before eleven o'clock.

div.head: NEW GYMNASIUM.
div.p: THE NEW GYMNASIUM.

Op Tuesday evening the Mayor (Alderman T. 11. Sutton) opened what is now known as the War- rington Gymnasium, at the building formerly used as a irotkmen's Club. Amongst those present were the Revs. S. Wilkinson and T. Emmett, Messrs. T. Morris, J. E Wright, F. Monks, J. D. Buckton, J. Evans, J. Dunn, J. E. Warren, T. Pemberton, Ferguson and A. Alexander, director of the Liver- pool Gymnasium. .The building has been fitted with various modern conveniences for physical recrea- tion, amongst which are horizontal and parallel bars, vaulting horse and spring board, trapeze, swing rings, climbing rope, Ice. For the constitutionally weak, and the middle-aged, several machines, known as the Alexander chest expanders, the invention of Mr. Alex- ander, are provided. It is stated that one of those machines was recently made for Mr. Gladstone. The club will be open every Tuesday and Friday evening for men, and for *ladies, who will be instructed by Mrs. Alexander, every Friday afternoon. It is also intended to form a boys' class. The fee for membership is ss. per quarter. In opening the proceedings the Mayor said a Committee had been working hard for some weeks past to get up the gymnasium, and Mr. Alexander had paid several previous visits to the town for the purpose of assisting the Committee to make the arrangements for the opening, as well as to give them his valuable advice. (Applause.) The Committee found that there were gentlemen in Warrington who were desirous of supporting 'the gymnasium, provided the young men of the town also took an interest in it. Therefore its SUCCeSS entirely depended Upon themselves. Mr. Alexander had incurred considerable expense in fitt- ing up the apparatus, and he was deserving of their best thanks—(applause)—as were also the Committee who had worked with him. He proposed that a vote of thanks be accorded them for their valuable services. The motion was heartily agreed to, after'which the Mayor declared the gymnasium open.—Mr. Alexander then delivered a short address. He thought the Committee and himself had somewhat redeemed the promises they made, several months ago in the Drill Hall, by opening the eymnasium that evening. The Committee had acted wisely in mak- ing the present attempt a kind of feeler, although he had much faith that the institution would be a success. (Hear, hear.) The teaching would be in the hands of an experienced assistant—his chief assistant at Liver- pool—and he should occasionally be glad to come to Warrington to see how they wore getting on. In a short time, if the club prospered, various additions would be made. He had been bold enough to enter a team from Warrington to compete for the National Championship, although he had no idea they would win it the first year, but to enable them to gain expe- rience. The competition was somewhat similar to football championships, except that the prizes were much more valuable, and the exer- cise, although requiring equal skill and certainly more strength, did not possess that roughness which characterized football. The winning team received a shield into its keeping for 12 months of the value of £3OO, and each member of the winning eight received a shield for himself of the value of 25 guineas. (Applause.) He thought they might have a little competition of their own at the end of the present season, as well as an • assault-at-arms, and there was, therefore, plenty to emulate and encourage them. The gymnasium would be valuable for delicate persons, and those suffering from certain bodily ailments, and if they would come to the club he was sure they would receive a great amount of relief. It was proposed to have a class for boys, to serve as a sort of nursery for the evening class. Tuesday afternoon was at present suggested, and there would also be a class for ladies every Friday afternoon, under the management of Mrs. Alexander. There were no fewer than 300 ladies in the class in Liverpool, which was a great success.—Mr. F. Monks said that what they now Saw was a great advance upon what they saw as youngsters. As far as the success of the undertaking was concerned, that, of course, rested entirely with themselves, and if the members made it worth Mr. Alexander's while to come to Warrington to teach them, he felt satisfied that their townsmen would do what else was necessary. He hoped the members would make an effort to increase their numbers, be regular in their attendance at the practices, and that the prize giving would not be confined to either London or Liverpool. He had faith enough in the young men of Warrington to believe that after they had had a fair amount of train- ing they would be able to hold their own. He was willing to do all he could to assist the development of a sound mind in a amine body. (Applause.)—The Rev. S. Wilkinson also addressed the meeting, and wished the , institution success, believing that everything which I tended to increase physique was a good thing; he was i I also anxious to see a sound mind n a sound body. He should be willing to give a small subscription annually , towards the cost of the working of the gymnasium. (Applause.)—Mr. Smith, one of Mr. Alexander's assis- tants, then put a number of the new members through ' a variety of exercises of a very interesting character. About 60 persons have already become members of the I gymnasium.

LIVING WAXWORKS AT On Wednesday Wednesday evening an amusing entertain- ment was given by members of the Holy Trinity Church and friends, in aid of the Choir Fund. The proceedings took place in the sOhtyolroom, before a crowded audience, the , Vicar, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton,,presiding. The programme consisted of songs, humourous and sentirnenlat. by Mrs. Haddock, Messrs. Percy Davies, W. lohnson, Can- field, Westbrook, Riley, and the choir, who *ere ably accompanied on the piano by Mr, Evans, A. C. 0: A wonderful and most amusing exhibition of living waxworks was also shown by Professor Septimus Nosibor, (Mr. A. H. Robinson's, while last, but not least, Jumbo Junior, a wenderful performing elephant, was introduced among the figures, and a further novelty in the :shape of " Pongo, the monkey man," created an amused sf not startled sensation amongst the beholders. The showman was in good form and imitated very cleverly loquacity 1: and bumptiousness of the race of " Artemus." His ;graphic recital of the achievements, histories, and ;shortcomings of the occupants of his caravan, plenti- , fully interspersed with puns and topical allusions, wtss irresistible. The "show" was divided into three "Caravans" which comprised :—No. 1., Queen Elizabeth, Mary Queen of Scots, Evangeline Caller Herrin, Chinese Lady and Gentleman, Robinson'Crusoe, and the Siamese Twins. No, IL, Darby and Joan, Mother Shipton, Lady Macbeth, Grace Darling, Little Red Riding Hood, Joan of Arc and the Pirate Chief of the Sankey Sand Banks, together with Pongo, the Monkey Man. No. Squeers, Sleeping Beauty, Florence Nightingale, Jonas Hanway, Where are You going to, iinf Pretty Maid, Ally Sloper, and Pears'Soap with Jumbo jun „and the Performing Elephant. The incidental music was played by Miss Haddock, a grand fintde being given to the entertainment, by the simultaneous exhibition of the whole of the figures pre- viously shown. ,

"THE MESSIAH" AT THE PUBLIC , HILL. ; On Monday evening "The Messiah." was given in the Public Hall, as the second (extra) concert of the Warringkrn. Musical Society. There, was a I crowded attendance, except in the front seats, which were not so well filled as usual. This is much to be regretted, as the Society I had gone to great expense in procuring a full orchestra and first-class Principals, and those who were absent miss'ed what is regarded as the best performance the Society has given. The principal vocalists were Mademoiselle Ankinette. Trebelli (soprano), Miss Eleanor Rees (contralto), Mr. Henry .Piercy (tenor), and Mr. Bridson (bass). It is a Pleasure to be able to speak in almost unqualified terms of the manner in which Handers grand oratorio was performed. The mem- bers of the Society seemed' to be conscious that they had to redeem themselves, and the chorus certainly sang throughout with great power and fervour. The sopranos, in particular, distinguished themselves, especially in the choruses "And the glory of the' Lord," "Lift up -your heads," and " The Hallelujah," the volume of sound given forth being well sustained and homogeneous. The bass singers were, however, somewhat weak in the chorus "For unto us," but showed well in the final passage, " Blessing and honour." Speaking of the-chorus as a whole it must be said that they acquitted themselves admirably, the" Hallelujah" Chorus in particular being sung with energy and feeling seldom surpassed. The baisci, too, was better than could have been antibipated, considding that it was what might be called a "scratch" band got together for the occasion. There were some two dozen members in it, and three-fourths of the number, it is satisfactory to state, were local' players who showed themselves to be thoroughly efficient. Their accompaniments were in the main given with-taste and precision, and the way in- which the more delicate passages of "Every Valley," and the" Pa.storni-Symphony,' were played was ample evidence of theft- being equal to the task assigned them. It would be well' if arrangements could be made whereby the services of this, or a similar band, could be secured for every performance of the Society. Coming to the princliSals, it is to be noted that Mademoiselle Antoinette Trebelli is possessed of a soprano voice'of remarkably good quality. Its range is above the average ; it is alike sweet and flexible, and' gives evidence of careful training. She made a good impression in the recitative "There were shepherds " she. was still more successful in the air " Come unto Him" ;:and was all that could be wished in theme air "I' know that my Redeemer liveth," her rendering, of which 'cv,s loudly applauded. Of Miss Eleanor Rees it is requisite to say that she is a vocalist of the very highest order. She has a powerful organ, which is well under control, and which is at all times sweet as -well as sonorous. She sang "Behold, a Virgin "in a manner which raised expectations, and the expectations were by nomeans disappointed, for, when she proceeded with the air " Oh, thou that teliest," it was perceived that Ihdidel's noble music would be adequately rendered so far as she was concerned. Her singing of "He shall feed His flock" was soulful and beautiful, while the deepest pathos was expressed in the air "Hb was despised and rejected." In these passages, Miss- Rees may be said to have taken the audience by storm; end there was a desire to insist on an encore, notwithstancling that it would have been a breach of the proprieties in such a perform- ance as "The Messiah,. Whenever Miss Rees again appears in Warrington she will be sure to attract listeners. Mr. Piercy was found to be a singer of more Mtn ordinary power and breadth of expres- sion. This was seen as he led off with "Comfort ye my people," and (specially in the noble air "Behold, and see." He sang i "1 hou shalt break them," with great vigour and. with great feeling, and it is a matter of course to sav that he was heartily cheered. Mr. Bridson is a well-trained and experienced bass. He is just a trifle hard and mechanical at times, but for the most part he delivered himself with excellent effect, and was therefore highly appreciated His greatest success was with the air, "Why do the nations rage," which was rendered with sustained declamation. Mr. E. Townsend Driffield and Mr. W. S.. Woods, as accompanists, were all that could be desired ;. and With regard to the conductor, Dr. Hiles, it is due to say that be exercised the utmost care to make the best of the opportunity and is deserving of credit for the greatsuccess of the performance. The concert closed soon after ten o'clock, leaving an impression upon all who heard it that if" The Messiah" could always be so excellently performed; it would be well if its production became an annual institution.

OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATION. BUCKINGHAM PALACE. .

The large sheet two-colour Almanac which we present to our readers with this week's issue of the " Examiner " is adorned, it will be observed, with a finely-finished engraving of Buckingham Palace, and a faithful portrait of Her Majesty the Queen. The history of Buckingham Palace goes back nearly three hundred years. To begin at the be- ginning,we find ourselves soon after I he accession of James I.,in the ferns is Mulberry Gardens,which the British Solomon established with the view of intro- ducing silk culture on a large scale into England. _ The Mulberry Gardens—the site of the present Buckingham Palace and its gardens—do not appear to have had much consequence in an industrial sense, as might be expected, considering the nature of the climate. The office of Keeper of the Mul- berry Gardens became something of a sinecure, and evidently not of much value, for it is recorded that one of the officials sold it for the sum of .£406 to George Goring, a favourite of the King. Goring, -created a peer in 1628, built a house adjoining the Gardens. The property. after having been held by the Earl of Arlington, passed into the possession of John Sheffield, Marquis of Normandy, who in 1703 was created Duke of Normandy, and shortly after- wards Duke of the County of Buckingham. " Buck- , ingham," as he preferred to sign himself, received an additional grant of land from the Crown, pulled down the old mansion, arid built in 1703 the red brick pile hereafter known as Buckingham House. The Duke of Buckingham took enormous pleasure in the building of his House; and both he and Daniel Defoe have described the house and grounds in loving detail. " Under the window," writes tile owner, "there is a little wilderness full of blackbirds and nightingale's." He married Lady Catherine Darnley, one of the children of James 11. ; and after his death, in 1721, his widow wanted £60,000 for the house, which the then Prince of Wales and Princess of Wales strongly desired. The widow survived her husband till 1743. In 1761 the property was bought from Sir Charles Herbert Sheffield, the heir of the Duke of Buckingham, by Geo. 111., for £21,000, and subsequently "Buckingham House, now called the Queen's House," was settled by Act of Parlia- ment on Queen Charlotte, instead of Somerset House. George 111. established in the House an immense and valuable library, which Samuel Johnson had access to, and concerning which the great lexicographer, who had an interview with the young King, remarked, ace riling to Boswell, "that it was more numerous and curious than he supposed any person could have made in the time which the King had employed." Buckingham House became the private town residence of George 111. and his consort ; and here the Queen gave birth to all her four- teen children ,with the exception of George IV. After the death of Queen Charlotte, the King removed to Windsor, where he lived in gloomy and unhappy seclusion, and Buckingham House fellinto dust and decay. SOOR after George M.'s death, in 1820, between sixty and seventy thousand of the volumes which formed the library at Buckingham House were removed by an arrange inent with George IV. to the British Museum, where they at present remain and form a very important part of that great collection. George IV. afterwards conceived the scheme of making Buckingham Palace the headquarters of the Court instead of St. 'James', and the proposal was made to Parliament, which grudgingly granted the necessary funds. Nash, the King's favourite architect, was employed; the works were commenced in 1825 and completed about 1828. Subsequently enormous sums were spent, and the work of re-modelling was not completed till a short time before the happy accession of her Majesty. During the whole of the reign of William IV. the process of altering and re-modelling went on, and, just before Queen Victoria came to the Throne, the New Palace was considered to be so inadequate as a Royal residence that still further alterations were made, after designs by Blore, and a new front was built. It is calculated that the cost of the Palace itself, up to the Queen's accession, includ- ing the architectural after-thoughta, but exclusive of the expense of furnishing, has been £673,777. Whatever may be said about the external appearance of Bucking- ham Palace—a place which it was once said, was built for one kin.. and furnished for another—no fault can be found with the interior, the rich glories of which have excited unbounded admiration. All the resources of art have been drawn upon forthe decoration of this royal abode. Here is a description of the Throne-room, as it appeared shortly after her Majesty's accession i—" The Throne-room, 64ft. in length, presents a blaze of elabor- ate enrichment. The walls are hung with crimscn satin,! striped; and the alcove on the north side with crimson velvet, relieved with a profusion of gilding, and emblaz- onry of arms, Pee. The fascia consists of massive gilt wreaths, and two Large figures bearing a gilt medallion of George IV. In this recess is placed the Royal Throne, with Chair of State. The ceiling of the room is coved, richly emblazoned with arms, and gilded in the boldest Italian style of the 15th century. Beneath is a white marble frieze, exquisitely sculptured by Bailey —the design, the Wars of the Roses, Stothard's last great work. In this room are presented addresses to the Queen in State as picturesque as it is splendid." It was at Buckingham Palace, on the 13th of July, 1837, that Queen Victoria took up her residence, and four days afterwards went to open Parliament in state. The Palace was frequently used in state ceremonials. Buck- ingham Palace was a favourite abode of the Royal pair, and Prince Albert took great interest in the laying out of the graunds and procuring aquatic birds, which acquired extraordinary d9cility. The Princess Royal was born at Buckingham Palace, and in February, 1841, was christened in the Throne Room that we have just des- cribed. The water used for the ceremony—as in the case of a recent christening of the first-born of her Majesty's youngest daughter—was brought from the river Jordan. The Prince of Wales was born at Buckingham Palace on the 9th November, 1841, and the christening this time took place in St. George's Chapel, Windsor, on the 25th of January.lB42. On the 12th of May, 1842, the Queen, with the object of giving a stimulus to trade in London, gave a bal tnasqui at Buckingham Palace, and appeared herself as Queen Philippa, consort of Edward 111., while Prince Albert assumed the character of Edward ITI. There have been many distinguished visitors at Buckingham Palace, the principal, perhaps, being the autocrat Czar Nicholas and the ill-starred Louis Phillippe. The Emperor of Russia arrived at Woolwich on the Ist of June, 1844, and in honour of the visit great festivities were held at Buckingham Palace and Windsor. Mendela- sahn, who visited the Palace during the lifetime of the Prince Consort, in a letter to his mother, observed, "It is the one retlly pleasant and thoroughly com- fortable English house where one feels a son else.' The history of Buckingham Palace as a Royal resort has, during the Queen's widowhood, been a comparative blank, and it is only on rare occasions that it is used by her Majesty.

MR. TOMICINSON AT KINGSLEY.—A meeting of the Liberals of the Kingslet polling district was held in the National Schoolroom on Monday evening, when an -address was delivered by Mr. James Tomkinson, of .Willington Hall. Mr. Peter Hall presided, and in the course of a few introductory remarks said that Mr. TOrnkinson's presence there that evening as a Liberal landlord was, in his (the Chairman's) opinion, almost a curiosity. Mr. Tomkinson, who was accompanied by Mrs. Tomkinson, and further supported on the platform by Mr. B. Kniveton and Mr. Clegg, of Runcorn, spoke at considerable length on the Irish land question and several other topics included in the Liberal pro- gramme of future reforms. Mrs. Tomkinson, in respond- ing to a request fOr a speech, spoke a few words on the evictions that had recently taken place, and were still progressing in Ireland. Mr. Clegg was called upon by the Chairman, and his humorous remarks elicited much merriment. Afterward a vote of thanks was moved by Mr. S. Woodward to Mr. and Mrs. Tomkinson, and seconded by Mr. E. Alderman, which was heartily res- ponded to. Me. Tomkinson, in returning thanks, proposed a like compliment on behalf of the Chairman (Mr. Hall), which was seconded by Mr. Clegg and serried. RATEPAYERS' MEETING.-A special meeting of the rate- payers of the township of Frodsham was held in the Overseers' office, Frodsham, on Thursday morning.- On the motion of Mr. Ashton, seconded by Mr. Tiley, the senior overseer was voted to the chair. The retiring assistant overseer (Mr. R. Andrews) read the notice call- ing the meeting, which was for the purpose of consider- ing the assistant overseer's letter resigning his office on the 31st inst. for electing a successor, and for fixing the amount of sa:lary, for such officer.—Mr. John Ashton moved, and Mr. R. Bate seconded,that the salary remain as heretofore, viz., £5O per annum. This on being put to the vote was carried unanimously, a member remark- ing that a good man could not be got for little money. The meeting then proceeded with the following nomin- ations of persons who were considered as eligible persons for the vacant office —Mr. H. Tiley, proposed by Mr. John Forster, seconded by Mr. W. Youd : Mr. W. McWaters ; proposed by Mr. W. Booth (farmer), seconded by James McWaters ; Mr. J. Frodsham (Aston), proposed by Mr. W. J. Booth, seconded by Mr. W. Rodgers; and Mr. Geo. Jones, proposed by Mr. H. Clough, seconded by Mr. John Challoner. The follow- ing is the result of the show of hands :—Mr. Tiley, 8 votes ; Mr. McWaters, 4; Mr. Frodsham, 3; Mr. G. Jones, 11. A poll havin,y, been demanded on behalf of each of the candidates, the Chairman declared that the Meeting was adjourned.
