HOMELESSI CHILDREN.

Sir,—Homeless—Hungry—Cold. Threeterrible words, happily conveying but small meaning to most of your readers. Here in the great city, however, we are daily reminded that helpless children are only too vividly acquainted with their meaning in its bitter fulness. Our .rescued family in their sixteen Homes now number nearly 400, and they range in both sexes from babies to youths and maidem of sixteen and seventeen. They earn more than a fifth of the entire income of the in- stitution by their own industries, but at this season of the year we have special need in the'way of extra food and clothing, and the cold of winter always drives many more waifs and strays to our door. May we ask the generous help of your readers'? The children can help by collecting round the table at breakfast or dinner on Christmas Dav—sending us the result. Five shillings will support a homeless waif for one week in these Homes; 255. a month, or £l5 a year. A family might well be represented by a poor child thus entirely sup- ported. Parcels of cast-off clothing, especially over- coats and warm underwear, are greatly needed; also toys, new or old, Christmas cards, tcc. Parcels and letters should be addressed clearly anci con- tain name and address of senders.—Yours,
LEONARD K. SHAW. 1 Hon. Sees. • GILBERT R. KIRLAW. Boys' and Girls' Refuges and Homes, - Frances-st., Strangeways.
RAINHILL ASYLUM AND PENSIONS.

Sir,—lt surely canyot be true that the county propose,l amongst other things, to pension their chief medica officer, in the prime of life, with eight hundred pounds per year! And yet this is what the Liverpool and Man- chester 'tapers say. If such be the proposed pensions it would b6interesling to know what his salary has been, exclusive of house, garden, vegetables and all other advantages as seem to surround such posts. I have seen it stated that his salary is £l,OOO per year, indepen- dent of all c her advantages, and it does seem a pity to j bring the pension down £2OO a yea!: 1 Wiiy not continue' the £l,OOO per year AS a pm;ion for the next possible twenty years, for it is remarkable that pensioned servants don't die off, as other people do ? I see a large and influential meeting has been pre- sided over bv the Mayor of Heywood to pfotest against such misappropriation of ratepayers' money, and I trust that meetings will be held in every town in Lanca- shire to protest against would-be generous and benevo- lent men giving away the ratepayers' money, without consulting them. . . _ _

If his past services had not been esteemed and ap- praised at their full value, I take it that Dr. Rogers would have pointed that out to the :Committee of Jus- tices, and they would have at once given him what was a fair equivalent for his services; or I think I may venture to suggest, if he could have seen the way during the past few years to obtain any other appointment with larger emoluments, he would hardly have per- mitted his love for the lunatics to prevent his acceptance of it. If I am right in my conclusions, where should the pension come ih ? • We are not having County Councils a day too soon, and it does not look very graceful to saddle the coming Council with a burden of this kind. The whole thing looks very like what is commonly called a job.—Yours obediently,
RATEPA YER.
"WHO I'AYS RITES r

Sir,—Readers of the strange medley of personal abuse and misquotation, which appeared in yourlast week's paper above the signature of Mr. Thornton, might well be excused for overlooking how miserably he fails to sustain the arguments he put forward in his first letter. Finding that he cannot maintain an untenable position, he falls back on the old device of drawing off behind a cloud of words. To illustrate my contention that rates were generally really a deduction from ground rents, I mentioned a case, supplied by Mr. Thornton himself, in whieh the value of a shop site inWarrington had,through the growth of the trade and population of the town, increased by £4O a year. Out of this £4O something over £ll is paid in rates • and, therefore, I pointed out that this £ll was really a'deduction from ground rent— a deduction from an increased annual value which had been conferred upon the site not by the owner himself, but entirely by the town as a whole. In reply, Mr. Thornton said that the £ll could not be a deduetion. from the ground rent as the ground rent had been "unalterably fixed" when the site was taken on a lease of 999 years some years ago. This reply of Mr. Thorn- tort displayed an ignorance of a simple economic fact which is not to be excused in a gentleman who thought himself fit to be a town councillor. I, of course, pointed out to him, that ground rent "is the rent which is, or can be, obtained for allowing the use of a site of land," and that, according to his own showing, the annual value of this particular site had increased by £4O a year, out of which only about £ll were taken as rates. To this he can find no further reply than that his "state- ment was that land leased for 999 years was unalterably fixed by law for that term," the bearing of which on the argument I leave the reader to find out.

Thornton further argued that rents are dependent on-rates, that is to say, that when rates rise rents rise also, and that when rates fall renos fall. I, thereupon mentioned a recent case of a rise of 3d. a week in the rents of cottages, a rise which is equal to about 10d. in the £ on the rates,rand I asked him to point out when there had been a raising of the rates by 103. in the £ to cause this rise of rent. What is his answer? The only answer he attempts to makeis that, perhaps, the rents of the cottages had been previously lowered by 3d. a week and the pre:,ent rise was only bringing them back to the old figure. This is not the case, for the rents of the cottages had never been lowered from the time they were built. But, taking Mr. Thornton's answer as it stands, is it not a conclusive proof, that he really does not know what he is arguing about. For if rents are dependent on rates, as Mr. Thornton says they are, there must have been a corresponding reduction of 10d. in the £ on the rates, to permit of the lowering of the rents by 3d. a week; yet nobody knows better than Mr. Thornton that there has been tie such reduction of rates within the last few years. The clear inference from this is, then, that Mr. Thornton „so little under- stands the argument he rashly took uplhis pen to refute that he actually himself gives an explanation which is as fatal to his own theory as the original instance was. What does Mr. Thornton mean when he says "it seems-wanting to imagine even that he is not a -wealthy man, seeing that he is an Economist and so exceptibe, ally accomplished?" Does he intend to. maintain that accomplishments and the scraping together of money always go together? I should have thought that a busi- ness man of Mr. Thornton's experience would have been one of the last to put forward a proposition of that kind. He cannot be unaware of the fact that many in whom even the m3st charitably disposed has never detected the slightest trace of any one of those qualities or acquire- ments which are generally supposed to entitle a man to be considered accomplished, have yet, by means more or less obvious, succeeded in accumulating wealth. In fact, so far from this new proposition of Mr. Thornton having any truth in it, there are men who are rich because they are not accomplished. Had they been I accomplished they would not have been rich; Burns tells 1 us to—

"Gather gear by every wile That's justified by honour." Accomplishments do not lead a man to despise theadvice contained in the first line of this couplet, but they cer- tainly strengthen his determination to abide by the con- dition in the second. And some fortunes would never have been made had it been necessary to justify every addition to them by even the laxest code of honour. - 'I had intended to commentupon some of what I might call the curiosities of Mr. Thornton's last letter, but I find I have already taken up considerable space. There is, however, just one point to which I should like to revert. I have before complained that M. Thornton is addicted to misquotation, and allow ma to give a single instance of his honest method of carrying on a con- troversy. In my article I said, "the fact is that wereall the rates abolished to-day the rent-payers of Warrington would not benefit by a single penny. The demand for houses continuing, rents would renfain exactly as they are, and, if that demand continued to grow. rents would rise in spite of the non-existence of rates. The whole benefit of the abolition of rates wauld be enjoyed by that small and, ass rule, very comfortably provided for class who own the ground plots of Warrington." In place of the above Mr. Thornton quotes me as writing "that if rates were abolished it would neither effect property owners nor occupiers, but simply the landowners.' This is not only not a literal quotation, as Mr. Thornton would make it appear, but it is not even a decent summary. If it were intended as a summary, it again shows that Mr. Thornton does not understand the subject he is writing about.—Yours, &c., ECONOMM.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday forenoon. There were present Mi .J. Kenwright (chair- man), the Rev. S. A. .K. Sylvester, Messrs. W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, J. Leatherbarrow, W. Middlehurst, R. A. Grayes, J. Fisker, J. Ranson, J. Whalley, P. Longton, J. Birchall, W. Swift, J. Burchall, J. Ellison, W. Twist, J. Buckley, J. Griffiths, J. Mercer, E. Syder, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). INMATES.—The Master reported that there were 573 inmates in the workhouse this week, 568 last week, and 536 in the corresponding week last year. There had been 47 vagrants relieved during the week, against 59 in the corresponding week fast year. . . . _
, . ~ AN APPOINVAINT.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the appointment of Mr. R. G. Waterman, as school attendance and inquiry officer for the Woolton district.

TER GUARDIANS AND Si'. HELENS CORPORATIONir—ID accordance with notice given, Mr. James Burchall moved "That the sum of £4O per annum be off2red to the St.. Helens Corporation, to secure the admission, treatment, maintenance, &c., in their. Infectious Diseases Hospital, of all pauper cases of infectious diseases arising within the Borough of St. Helens, the said £4O to cover all charges." He remarked that the original notice of mo ion was given by their late respected member Mr. Lowe and he regretted the necessity for him to have to take it up in Mr. Lowe's place. He explained that the Guardians had originally intended to erect a large infectious diseases hospital to deal with all cases which might arise in the Union but the Local Government Board declined to grant them permission to do so on the ground that it was not the duty of the Guardians to protect the health of the district, arid they had no power to build an infectious hospital. That scheme had to be given up, and negotiations were entered into with the St. Helens Corporation in reference to the admission of pauper cases int. their hospital, but they resulted unsatisfactorily. The sum now mentioned was based on a calculation of the Corporation medical ()Meer, and he thought it would prove about right. He trusted the motion would be carried unanimously so that they would have no longer the scandal of the poor fever patient suffering while two great Boards were wrangling about a few, coppers.—Mr. Tyrer, hi seconding the motion, said if they could get rid of the friction that had arisen between the Board of Guardians and the Corporation, it would be a very pleasant way of getting out of the difficulty.—Mr. Mercer thought they should make arrangements for other portions of the district, and not one portion alone.—The motion, after further discussion, was adopted,,. _ .

THE COMPLIXENTS OF 'THE SEASON.—The Chairman said that as he would not meet them again before Christmas was passed, he wished them all a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. (Hear, hear.) CoyreacTs.—The following contracts were accepted : —Flour' &c., Thomas Seddon, Prescot ;groceries, James Povey, St. Helens ; butter, cheese, and eggs, John Collins, St. Helens; wine and spirits, Wildock and Son; linen and woollen drapery, Jos. Huyton, Liverpool; leather, Messrs. Poocock Bros., London ; boots and shoes, 0. Heneman, St. Helens; coals, R. Evans and Co., Haydock ; ironmongery, R. G. Brook, St, Helens; earthenware, H. Webb, St. Helens ; brushes, School- for the Blind, Liverpool ; coffins, Jos. Craven, St. Helens ; meat, Wm. Wilcock and Son, Liverpool. The proceedings then terminated.
COUNTY COUNCIL. IitTNCOTIX DIVIBIM.

Mr. Philip Speaknan has now announced himself as a candidate for Runcorn North. and in our advertisement columns, will be found his address, which fully explains the grounds upon which he appeals to the electors. It is to be regretted that his opponent, Mr. W. IL Linaker, is at present suffering from a severe cold and is confined to the house. Notwithstanding many rumours and statements to the contrary, Major flazlehurst, it is said, will be in the field in the course of a few days, and then there will be three candidates for the one seat. Mr. Brundrit's position in Runcorn South is still unn ssailed.

selected, as well as the deputy chairman of the Quarter Sessions, and who would probably be equally influential in the coming Council. The member of Parliament for the division recently recommended that the election should be non-political, knowing full well that Widnes proper, if not exactly Radical, was thoroughly Liberal, and that it was perfectly certain a Liberal would be elected on political grounds. Upon non-political grounds they could get a good Liberal to represent them as well as a good Conservative like Mr. Bleckly. He argued that they ought to get a representative from amongst throe gentlemen who had a more immediate and dirt interest in Widnes than Mr. Blackly, and he proposed that the Board recommend the ratepayers to adopt Mr. Mt spratt as a candidate. The Chairman said all they had to do as a Board was to set the ball rolling. In reply to Mr. C. Taylor, the Chairman said the gentleman he had intended tosuggest would not allow his name to be put in nomination. Mr. Carey agreed with Mr. Gaskell that they ought to endeavour to keep party politics out of the County , Council as they had succeeded in keeping them out of the Local Board. With regard to Mr. Muspratt, Mr. Gaskell must have been misinformed. The Liberal party had not made any move or adopted Mr. Muspratt, or any other candidate. He had a conversation with Mr. Muspratt on the previous day, and Mr. Muspratt said very distinctly that if be was the nominee of Widnes he would wish to represent the town not as a party man—not as a Liberal or Radical,—but he would endeavour and it would be his desire to be sent as the representative of the whole of the ratepayers. He (Mr. Carey) would rather see a representative of Widnes who was locally connected with the district, than an outsider, however eminent or suitable. He bad the utmost respect for Mr. Meekly, and they were all indebted to him for his efforts on their behalf, but he thought Mr. Muspratt would be a better representative for Widnes and he seconded Dr. O'Keeffes motion.
The motion was carried without dissent, Mr. Gaskell declining to vote —Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. Carey, Handley, Taylor, and T. S. Timmis were appointed a deputation to wait upon Mr. Muspratt.
MR. MIISPRATT CONSENTS.

The deputation appointed have waited upon Mr. Muspratt, who has consented to allow his name to be nominated. Party politics will be carefully avoided, and a representative committee will be formed to secure Mr. Muspratt's election. _

div.head: MEETING AT STRETTON.

A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. J. Charlton Parr for the Appleton division was held in the Schoolroom, Stretton, on Monday evening. Mr. Thomas H. Lyon' J.P., occupied the chair, and was suppor ed by Mr. b. Logan Wright, Ur. R. H. Kerr, Mr. Joseph Cliffe, Mr. Henry Greenall, and Mr. W. B. Roberts. There was a large attendance. Amongst the audience, which included several-ladies, were Messrs. John Tinsley, J. C. Calvert, Thomas Hewitt, Charles Whitley, William Fletcher, Edward Brocklehurst, William Winstanley, Alfred Barber, Alfred Faulkner, Hugh Darbyshire, John Darbyshire, Thomas Hindley, John Ellison, and George Barber. After an address byMr.- Parr, Mr. R.N. Kerr moved a rezolution in favour of the return of Mr. Parr. Mr. J. Cliffe seconded the proposal which was *so, sup- ported by Mr. D. Logan Wright, and Mr. W. div.head: DARESB-CRY DIVISION.
div.p: DARESB-CRY DIVISION.

A meeting of ratepayers was held at Halton last nigct week, to consider the representation of the Dares- bury Division in the County Council. Mr. Thomas Wright was voted to the chair.—Mr. John Baguley pro- posed that Mr. Joseph Stokes, farmer, of Rock Savage, 'be nominated a candidate. Mr. Stokes was a 'arc' a:- , hearted, good all round man, who would know how to spend the patepayers' money, and was in every way qualified for the position of County Councillor.—Mr. George Leathwood seconded the motion.—The chairman thought if Mr. E. Greenall was approached in a nice manner, he might withdraw in favour of Mr. Stokes, and he should be pleased to ask him to do so. 'He felt certain that in face of Mr. Stokes, Mr. Greenall would not have the slightest chance, and that they would not dave the slightest difficulty in placing their friend at the head pf the poll, even if Mr. Greenall did come forward. —Mr. Haddock said he had signed a requisition to Mr. Lialker, but he should vote for Mr. Stokes now.—Mr. William Stokes, brother to the proposed candidate, Said it was an abominable shame that they had to pay such heavy rates in that township. They were not poor rates, they were gentlemen's rates. (Laughter.) People who did not own a wheelbarrow had to pay highway rates (Laughter.) He was sure his brother would do his best for everyone.—The motion was passed, and a deputation consisting of Messrs. J. Baguley, Ackerley, Astbury. Leathwood, and John Lucas, was appeinted to wait upon Mr. Stokes.

div.head: WIDNES DIVISION.
div.p: WIDNES DIVISION.

SELECTION OF A CANDIDATE. On Tuesday evenin,g a special meeting of the members of the Widnes Local Board was held at the Town Hall for the purpose of considering the representation of V. idnes on the County Council of Lancashire. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided and there were present Dr. O'lieeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley, D. Wright, B. Brown, R. Cook, F. Reyes, H. Gasket! sun., J. Houghton. S. Saddler, J. Taylor, W. W. Gossage, J. Midwood and J. T. Allen (clerk). —The Clerk said the Mowing letter addressed to the Chairman had been received that afternoon:—

"Dear sir, as lunderstand you- rlitxtrd meets this after- noon, to discuss the question of the election of a County Cbuneillor, I bpg to state that I and several other rate- payers have sounded Mr. Muspratt as to his becoming a candidate. Although expressing himself as not anxious to serve, I have no doubt Mr.. Muspratt would consent to become a candidate if he learned that such were the wish of any considerable number of ratepayers. As there can be no doubt of Mr. M'uspratt's peculiar fitness for the position, I venture to think that an influential deputation should wait uporr him and solicit his per- mission to be nominated. If desired I shall have much pleasarein forming, one of _the-deputation. Yours faith- fully, T. Sutton Timm's."

said: he had been informed—he did not know whether it was true--that the Liberal Association proposed to run Mr. Muspratt.. His own feeling was that neit' her of the political associations ought to take an active part in this election. He thought politics had been the.ruin of our Town Chuncil work to a great extent • and he a/so thought they in Widnes had been particularly fortsmate in the- way politics had been excluded in the selection of members of the Local Board. Holding. these views, and feeling that Widnes owed a I very great debt of gratitude to. Mr. /3leckly for the way in. which he had fought their battle for a second repre- sentative., he had endeavoured. tn. privately ascertain if he would become a candidateibr Widnes if requested tn do so. He had received the %Rowing letter in reply.• • " Altrincl33.ce, 2nd December, 1888 Dear Mr. Gaskell„ lam much obliged for your kind letter andif I had arli ' intention of seeking a seat on the County Council, should have the greatest pleasure in representing tile constituency- or Widnes. 1- feel that the Quarter Sessicas have you a very great wrong„and have violateol.the- principle of the "Representation of the People Axt 1824.... by practically disfranchising 10,000 "capable citizens" as Mr. Glaastonsealled them in those days ; and / should have liked to carry on the contest to the titter end, but I came to the conclusion sometirae- ago that I must leave to younger men thework of the County Council, and I have so mach faith in the goodness of your cause and in the future of the County Council that have no doubt they will do you the justice which the quarter sessions refuse‘.l.--Yostrs faithfully H. Blecklyi" Mr. Haskell thought that if Mr. Bleckly got a practically unanimous invitation he might be-induced to stand. They could not possibly get a bettor candidate. He was deputy chairman of Quarter Sessions, ono of the senior magistrates of the division, and was one who was well acquainted with County work. If in were elected he would be at once elected an alderman, and probably chairman or vice-chairman of the Council, and Widnes could then choose a second councillor. These of the Conservative persuasion were likely to. be in predomin- ance on the Council, and therefore if they sent a repre- sentative who was an extreme Radical he would be like a red rag to a bull, and he would not be a member likely to be made an alderman, and they would lose their chalice of a second councillor. . . .

Mr. Reyes poizated out that if the question was to be. non-political any reference to a man's •polities should be left out ,and inseleeting a candidate they must crmsider whether he would be acceptable to the whole constituency. Dr. O'Keeffe said if the question of politics had to be excluded from the election, there were many good men who had a local interest in the town who might be

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
LYAOI.

The pump which has been put to work at the sewage farm portion of the Ship Canal works at Lymm did its work of draining the cutting in a remarkably short time, and it has now been removed back to the yard at Grappenhall. The cutting is now free from water, and the working is again in active operation. An embank- ment has been thrown up as a protection against floods. THE POMONA PALACE ARBITRATION. Mr. Daniel Watney, the arbitrator in :the case of Reilly v. Manchester Ship Canal Company, which occu- pied seven days at Manchester, has issued his aviard. The enquiry was held to assess the value of the property at Manchester known as the Pomona Palace and the Agricultural Hall, with grounds and adjoining. property. The property is valued by the claimant's witnesses at sums varying from £141,774 to £154,810, and by the Canal Company's ,witnesses at sums varying from £43,868 to £49,880. The compensation awarded by the arbitrator is £70,352. AcToN GRANGE WALTON Sze.

The Acton Grange Section has been fairly busy during the past week, the weather having been on the whole. alrotirabla. Further on at Walton tivo American navvies are engaged hi removing what was •lately the right bank of the cutting at a quick rate. Between Twenty Step Bridge and the Chester-road,a large number of men are engaged in filling, up the Old Quay canal to a third of its width with sand, taken from where the large steam navvy worked. There is' nowhere an embankment wholly across the coursq of this canal as it is not desirable to stop the free passage of the water until the canal is diained. WESTON.

Under the skilful care of Dr. Mangan, Mr. Weston the agent for this section is nicely recovering from his recent accidebt He has resumed his responsible duties at Weston Point, and work on the section is proceeding very briskly. During the past week a French Navvy has been fitted up, and commenced operations on the Marsh on Tuesday. There is now a large quantity of machinery employed in the cutting which has assumed very exten- sive dimensions, and the amount of material daily removed is tremendous. At the entrance to the Weaver great activity is displayed in laying the foundation for the great lock, and much progress is made weekly. MINSTRELS AT WESTON.

On Tuesday even-iii;111-E;s1;Cp Canal Minstrels gave an entertainment in thtZ Wesleyan Schoolroom; Weston. There was a fair attendance of the public. Since their last appearance the minstrels had matured the style and had introduced several new features, and their perform- ance was very attractive and entertaining. The corner men, Messrs. Tate and Bann, evolved a number of new jokes, which met with undoubted appreciation and these " artistes" were equally successful in their rende;t ~ - in of several songs. Songs were Also+ Fiven by Messrs. J. Jeffs, Thorpe, R. C. Rosenberg, and. Williams. The last named sang "Love's Request," in fine style. Mr. Beckett contributed a stump speech widen convulsed the audience with laughter and the performance concluded with the mirth provoking farce " Waxination Gratis." The duties of interlocutor were fulfilled by IV.R. Clarke.

div.head: HOOTON HALL ARBITdATIVN.
div.p: THE HOOTON HALL ARBITdATIVN.

Mr. Beads!, M.P., issued his award on Thntstkiy morn- ing in the arbitration which recently took place between Mr„Richard C. Naylor, of Hooton Hall,, and, the Man- chester Ship Canal Company. The case was, to assess the compensation to be pitid to Mr. Naylor in' respect to about 121 acres required for the Ship Canal under eking, and for the consequential damage to Hooton Ball and the adjoining estates. There was a further °ban for certain foreshore rights, the existence of whioh were partly disputed by the Canal Company. The • arbitra- tor awards in respect of the land taken and consequen- tiaf•damage the sum of £28,924, and a further smut of £1,835 if the right to the disputed foreshore. can be sustained. For the foreshore, about which there was no dispute, the arbitrator awards £2,578. In the evidence before the arbitrator the lowest sum plane} on the value of this property by the claimant was £82,811, of which £4,251 was in respect of the dispsted foreshore.

div.head: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT RIXTON. • Two PERSONS KILLED.
div.p: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT RIXTON. • Two PERSONS KILLED.

On Saturday morning John Barton, fireman, and James4kitton, roperunner,were being conveyed on the engine •" Lancaster," from the pay office at Rixton Ley to Theloran, when the engine left the rails and, runnoug up the-embankment, capsized, crushing the men fear- fully. They were at once conveyed to the hospital at Latchford, but Barton died before leaving the sc,,t, Cluttors, expiring a few hours after admittance.—On Monday. afternoon Mr. 11. C.. Yates, coroner, conducted an inrestigation at Latchford, as to the cause of din fatality.—Eridenee of identification having been given by relatives of the-deceased men, James 'Beard, driver of the engine "Lancaster," said he had been connected- with engines fen 20 years._ About half-past one on Saturday; he was in chargo of the "Lancaster," running from the pay-office at Rixtorr to Thelwall. There were on the engine beside himself„John Barton, his fireman,. James -Glutton,. reperunner, and two labourers from the German, navvy to. whom he was giving a "lift homo2'.' They had just been paid and were going hvie at the rate of about finm 12 to 15 miles per hour. About three or four haaulred yards from their starting place be- felt the engine-vim a leap ambit left the rails and, rune ning for about 20 yards alon., the embankment, turned over on its sida. Witness was thrown to some distance, but not hurt.. When he recovered himself he looked round for the. other men arid found the two deceased' underrthe engine, Barton under the 'tank and Clutten crushed by the penel. He inink,oed to push the engine oft thenr„andideag them out. There was another engine close behind them,and he cziled to the men forassistaace. The deceased, were placed upon this and conveyed. to- the hospital„ where it was found that the firm was dead,l mid.. the second man died soon after admission. He k afterwards went to look at the spot where the acckient :took place,,and he found that there was a wooden shoot i.uaning under the rails. This had leaked, the leakage ;caused a subsidence of the soil, and the road had suck. -1110 thought that the wei43t of the engine had caused the sea inking... He had been over the same road about seven b'clock thesame morning,and it was' then perfectlytlevol and.riOt. According to his experience the show% was tha usual mannor.—By a Juryman The-engine was going at its usual speed, and it was not the 'fact, as had been stated,that itt was going at a furious ra4..—Mr. Warlord, solicitor, Lyeam, who appeared on behnitof the widow of Clutton, ble permission of the Corcrensross- examined the wlineso, during which he said no sleepers were-torn up until the engine capsized. It. was impos- • sible for him to hate been going at a greaLsßeed, as he had only had from. three to four hundred yamls start. William Watts,. labourer, living at N. 0.. 11 Hut, ;Thelwall, who weer one of the men on the. engine at the time of the catastrophe, corroborated. rin. had had his hand crushed by the accident. _ .

, Mr. Charles 'rouse, agent in charge of No, 6 district,. said the Q.coident took place between. Sankey and Statham-Lanes. During the time of tho-flood about three weeks ago, a new pump had been laid down there, and the shoot hAd been carried under the.ralls between the sleepers. The shoot was made of new, wood,, and gave no suppoxt at all to the rails, 'with which it was con- nected. No water, had, however, passed down it dur- ing that week, as the pump had been removed, and, as the line had been in daily use/during that time, the subsidence could clearly not be due to leakage from the shoot. He was unable in any 'Sway- to account for the accident. It was not true that tho rails had sunk. He had examined the road and found it perfectly level. Six or sever platelayers were constantly employed upon that road, which was one of the best on the section. Beard had never been reported to him for furious driving.—By a juror: The road was perfectly guaged. The engine was a comparatively new one, and there was no impediment upon the road, Dr. Byrne, the resident medical officer at Latchford Hospital, deposed that the men were brought there on Saturday. Barton was quite dead, but Clutton survived for seveial hours, The latter was suffering from shock.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Earl of Warwick's condition was more encouraging on Friday. The Wellington statue erected in front of Apsley House, Hyde Park Corner, was uncovered by the Prince of Wales on Friday morning. A Central News Paris telegram says a man has been arrested at Havre on suspicion of having carried on a nefarious system of poisoning. • Colonel North has re-purchased Kirkstall Abbey from the gentleman who bought it last week, and has presen- ted the ruin to the town ef Leeds.
The Honourable Frederick Wynn, owner of the Glynllyfon estate, has undertaken to remit ten percent. to all his Canarvon,shire and Anglesey tenants paying tithes.

A large number of forged notes have recently been discovered in circulation in 'London. Something like a panic has been created, and the greatest difficulty is experienced by many people in getting notes changed. If there is an East End horror during the holidays we may also expect an arrest. The police are taking in- finite precautions to prevent a recurrence of the murders during the time which will offer peculiar temptations to the daring cunning of the murderer. GREAT FIRE AT A LANCASHIRR COTTON MILL.—A fire of a very destructive character occurred late on Thurs- day night at the mill of Messrs. Whittaker, cotton spinners and manufacturers, Hurst, near Ashton-under- Lyne. The fire continued to• burn until the morning was well advanced. The damage is estimated at £20,000, while 1,000 operatives will be thrown idle. The origin of the fire is unknown, TRAGEDY IN THE ISLE OF MAN.—Elizabeth Crowe, spinster, about forty-five years of fon, was discovered brutally mutilated about the head at daybreak oa Friday morning on a 'by-road off the highway from Ramsey to Laxey-. A stone covered with blood, by which it is supposed the murder was committed, was found near where the body had been dragged into the ditch. Deceased lived alone in a farmhouse. No motive for the outrage is known. FATAL ACCIDENT ON A LEEDS EXPRESS.—About noon on Friday a terrible accident occurred near Melton Mowbray, Leicestershire, to a gentleman travelling in the Puhnan car in the Leeds and Bradford express to London. There is a sharp curve, and as the express train was travelling at full speed a gentleman, whose name is not yet ascertained, was observed to be thrown by the lurch of the train from the car platform. He was killed instantaneously. STOCKTON-ON-TEES ELECTION. Sir Horace Davey (Gladstonian Liberal) and Mr. Thomas Wrightson (Con- servative) were nominated for . the Parliamentary vacancy at Stockton-on-Tees on Thursday. The polling commenced at Stockton-on-Tees yesterday (Friday). The Liberal Unionists worked hard for Mr. Wrightson, whilst Sir H. Davey had the aid of Alderman Richardson, a former Liberal Unionist. There was a heavy poll during the dinner hour, but the town was quiet. The poll was declared last evening as follows : DAVEY (L) 3889 WRMHTSON (C) 3494

• M.ajority 3911 The Liberal majority at the last election was 1002. Ma. Baroirr's ILtavEss.—Mr. Bright has improved dur- ing the tveek he has had a fairly good night on Wednesday, arid his condition remained about tie same on Thursday. Mr. Bright was much better on Friday morning, having passed a Very good night. •
MYSTERIOVS MURDER OF A WOMAN AT POPLAR.

IS IT ANOTHER WHITECHAPEL ATROCITY? The coroner for South-East Middlesex opened an inquiry at Poplar yesterday into the circum- stances attending the death of a woman unknown, whose body was found early. that morning in a place known as Clarke's Yard, High-street, poplar. Mr. Matthew Bromfield, the divisional surgeon of' the police, said he had made a post-mortem examination of the body, arra had found it to be that of a well-nourished woman about 30 years of age. Blood was oozing from her nostrils, and there was a slight abra.sion on the face.. Death was duo to strangulation. Witness did not think that deceased could have caused death herself. He thought the murderer must have stood at the left rear of the woman and having thrown a cord round her throat, across his hands, and so strangled her; After other evidence the inquiry was adjourned. A rumour prevails that the murder is the•work of "Jack the'Ripper." A telegram received late says the police are making fullest inquiries into latest Esst-end murder but without dis- covering any club. The opinion is expressed that the same miicreant is the author, although he has, changed his method of working..
A LETTER 510 M THE EXPLORER AND EMIN WELL IN AUGUST. (Reuter's Telegram.)

ZANZIBAR, DEC. 21.—A letter dated from Stanley Falls. August 29th, has reached here by Tippoo, Tib's man to-day stxting that on the preceding day a letter had been recsived from Stanley. He was then at Bonalya on the Arunwimi. He had met Emin Yeha 82 days previously in perfeet Health and with plenlrof food, and had lifmself returned for his rear guard and loads. He had arrived at llosalya on August 17, and intended leaving ten days later -presumably to rejoin Emin Pacha. All the white men of the expedition were in good health and..twantednot*ing. • , The latest comrannication Prom Stanley prior to tltat referred to in to-dr.yle telegrara was dated November a last year.
It should be recollelcted that the letter from Osman Digna, recently rece-Rmd by Genaral,Grenfell at Souakhn stated that EminPacha.and Stanley had surrendered on. October 10th

IPO THE COUNTY •ELECTORS OF THE 1 NEWTON-IN-MAKERFIELD DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF LANCASTU. LAMES AND GENTLEMEN.—The BOUDliary •Commissioners having constituted the townships of Newton-in-Makerfield and Ilaydock an Electoral Division under the Local Government Act of 1888, the duty will next month devolve upon-you of electing your representative to the County Council, A large and representative body of Ratepayers have invited me to become a Candidate, in opposition to the Nominee of a section of the joint meeting of tho Newton Commissioners and the Haydock Local Board, and I have accepted the invitation in the hope that I may, if elected, be of some service to you in your local affairs. The Local Government Act is a measure of the greatest importance to the country, and for the first time establishes the principle that in county government taxation should be accompanied by representation. It confers upon County Councils very large powers, which it is the intention of the Government, as early as possible, to extend to the Licensing question; and it places in the power of the Ratepayers a very large revenue from ordinary county taxation, supplemented by the proceeds of dates on local taxation licences, and a [portion of the Probate Duty—hitherto under the control of 'the Itoperial Exchequer. This additional revenue will, there- fore, to a certain extent, relieve local taxation. The Act is an honest endeavour to place local power in the hands of the Ratepayers, and this object will be further attained by its extension, next Sessibn, to the appointment of District Councils, whose work it will be to carry out all the details of Local Govermnent. Meantime, an additional amount of work will fall upon County Councils in carrying into effect the provisions of the Act, and organising a basis for its future satisfactory administration. It will be apparent that the labours of these Councils will- be of the highest importance, necessitating on the part of your Representative a close attention to his duties and an earnest endeavour to perform them in such a manner as to safe-guard your interests. If you should do me the honour to Elect me, I will give the requisite time and my best efforts to a careful considera- tion of the questions brought before me; I will in every possible way promote the welfare of the Division ; and it will be my object to secure for you a fair division of the funds to be appropriated to local affairs, and to keep down the local Taxes to the lowest point consistent with economy. As an employer of Labour and a Ratepayer for over twenty years, I have had experience which would guide me as to your necessities and wants, and I should -always be glad I ta receive any suggestions or help you might be able to give me. I am, I think, known to a large number of the Ratepayers, and hope to make the acquaintance of many more during my candidature. I look forward with pleasure to opportuni- ties of fut-ther addressing you, and entering more freely into my views upon the questions connected with County Govern- ment. , 'have the honour to be, Ladies and Gentlemen,' Your obedient Servant, GERALD W. RAWLINS.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. To THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTH DIVISION • OF RUNCORN. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—EIaving been requested by a large and influential body Of ratepayers to 6ffer myself as 'a candidate for this division, I have much pleasure in acceding ts their request. For the first time in the history of County Government, the ratepayers are now able to exercise a direct influence in the conduct and management Of local affairs. Underthe Local Government Act of last session, the new County Councils are entrusted with many matters of import- ance and responsibility, and in course of time there is little doubt that still further powers will be conferred upon them. It is therefore of the highest importance ithat your repre- sentative should be one who has an intimate knowledge of local requirements and of the best and most efficacious means of meeting such wants. Such a knowledge I claim to possess. Almost the whole of my lite has been spout amongst you, and as a ratepayer in the town for nearly 30 years, during which period I have also been a large employer of labour, I have been brought into close contact with all classes of the community and am thus well acquainted with their wants ;whilst my position as a Guardian of the Poor Coupled with sixteen years service as a Commissioner, constitutes an experience which cannot fall to be of value in the office for which I am now a candidate. Should I have the honour of being elected your represent- ative, I will do my utmost to further your interests in all respects, and It will ever be my aim to insure that the money paid hy you in the form of a County Rate shall be collected and expended equitably, judiciously, and economically. I have the honour to remitn, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your faithful servant, PHILIP SPEAKMAN. The Mount, Higher Runcorn, Dec. 18th. 1888.

CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTH DIVISION OF RUNCORN. LADIES and GENTLEMEN.—Some three weeks ago by a short paragraph in the local papers I pledged. myself to come forward as a candidate for this Division, in the new County Council, and I now by to confirm that announcement. The County Councils throughout the country have been called into existence in compliance with a demand which has from time to time been Urged 'upon successivr. Governments by all parties, the feeling generally being that the ratepayers Of the counties should have a voice in the election of some directly representative bodies which should have the control not only Of all &aunty property but also of the making, assessing, and levying of. all county, bridge, and other rates, which tip to the present time have been under the control of Quarter Sessions. This the neve Local, Government .Act— although imperfect in many ways—fully admits and pro- vides for. In the future the County Councils will have under their control the making and levying of all county, police and bridge rates, and the full control over all county property, from alike halls, and. assize courts, caunty asylums, reformatories and industrial schools, down to police courts. The Court of Quartet Sessions will retain little more than the administration of their criminal jurisdiction, appeals, etc. The police will be placed under the control of a joint com- mittee of a certain number of justices, and a certain number of members of the County Council. On this point as well as upon many others it will be neces- sary to see that the interests of the public are protected, and I think that by the direct representation which ratepayers generally will now obtain, many evils and petty annoyances will be removed. It is impossible in an address of this kind to touch upon all the powers conferred by the new Act upon the Council. and I have only referred to a few of the most important. My justification in asking you to support my candidature in this election is that from the public position in which I have been placed for many years in the connection with your local body of COmmissioners and the Runcorn Union, I have acquired a knowledge of local and county matters which will assist me materially inprotecting the interests of your Division, and of the district generally. I promise one thing, that nothing shall be done by the Council but what is thoroughly investi- gated and made known to the public. I have no personal interest in seeking your 'support ; I ask it in the interests of your Division. lam, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, W. If. LINAKER. 58, High-st., Runcorn;l3th December, 1888.

Neps is gooin' eawt o' fashion; istid o' geddin' a bunch for a penny, an' puttin' some Po' th' drawers to scent th' clooas, fooak gooa to th' druggist's shop, an' pay sixpence for a sooap o' stuff in a bottle hole th' size o' mi little finger. That's th' difrence between hem' genteel an' bein' sensible. Nein (—). Aw think mi "nabs" is same as sayin' "mi nebbur," bud aw'm nod sure. (To be kontinid.)

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. TEKKIN' TH' DOCTOR'S ADVICE. Owd Enoch o' Nabs wur a chap o' th' reight sooart, A rare hand at bullock, an' fond o' good spooart ; In his ways an' his tawk he wur booath foce an' droll, An wi' his own lot—a, convivial soul. He wur fond o' breawn ale; Amowd song, or a tale, 1 A pipe, or a slow fuddlin' stroll. He abs wur hearty, good-tempered an' gay, So wod Dame Misfortune mut put in his way; His words, drolly spokken, wur never unkind, Except, when fooak vexed him, he'd speyk eawt his mind. But to tek him o reawnd ; Among th' dwellers on t' greawnd, Another like him yo'd ne'er find. He'd jooak an' he'd laff ;—play sly tnarlocks, an' sing; Moear happy at heart than a Coourt-pampered King. He'd childer as liked him, an' as for his wife,— Owd Ailse,—hoo wur t!' comfort an' star ov his life. Tho' he oft sed her voice, When at him boo tried noise, NVur just like th' din ova crackt fife. I' his youtig days he'd frolicked, wi' o sooarts o' tricks, An' landed hisser into many a fix; But as age crope o'er him, it med him mooar staid, Heaw he gloried i' tellin' o'er th' marlocks he'd played; When among th' crony lot, • O'er a pipe, an' pint pot, I' gam, hey! he drooave a long trade He knew nowt o' th' doctors' rank nostrums, nod he, For he'd ailed nowt, except when he'd hed a good spree, But at last befell ill, an' hutched up ov a lump, Like a brid eawt o' sooarts ; an' wer numb as a stump. An' his wife sed, " Tha'rt pale, An' it's o thro' cowd ale ;" "Nay, nay, lass, mi marro' best' grump !" Ailse ans'red, "A doctor wod soon let thee know Wad ailment it is as is botherin' thee so ; Ged off wi' thee, do, he'll soon mend thee, thall see! Iv he doesnd, avv'm sure as thall varra soon dee. Go to th' doctor thisel, Then thi own tale thall tell : We dornd want to god shut o' thee I" So ho went to see th' doctor—a plain-spokken chap, As towd patients th' truth, an' ne'er keered a odd rap. He felt Enoch's pulse, an' examined his tongue, . Then towd him his liver an' inside wur wrong, "And mind, while you're ill, Of beer don't drink a gill. If you do, you will die before long !" He then geet some physic an' hobbled tort th' nest, Wheer he allus fun th' comfort as suited him best ; But afooar he reyched hooam, he just dropt, at th' street end, On a crony as bawled eawt, " Shape Enoch, an' mend; Tha looks powsy to-day, Come to th' pub across th way, Aw've a shillin' or two here to spend !" Wi' a bit o' persuadin', owd Enoch went in, • Whenhis mate sed" WoL's th' order,—rum, pooart wine, or gin ? ' "It's nowt !" moaned owd Enoch, as sad as cud be, "For th' doctor's just towd me aw mornd—doesta see! An' to blabber t' truth, Bill, Aw do feel sum an' ill, But, hang id! aw dornd want to dee !" Enoch sat quate a bit, an' pood slow at his pipe, Then sed, "Doctors o are like th' brids they co 'snipe' For wheerever one's sin it's a tidy long bill! • An' you mon ses plainly aw mornd hey a gill. But aw'm dry as con be; Aw mon sup,—Wod ?—let's see! Bring a pint o' t' best leatherheyd swill !" For a month or two Enoch refused every gill His mates offered. "Nowe, th' doctor ses me id 11 kill." But he supped tooathry pints, an' geet reawnd, hale an strung, A. hearty owd cock, seawnd i' body an' lung, An' sed, " Drinkin's nooan nice, Keep to th' doctor's advice, 'Dorn breyk id, or else yo'll do wrong!" Loup SALISISURY AT Ses.unonoron.—The Marquis of Salisbury arrived at Scarborough en Wednesday even- ing. In reply to an address of a very general character from the mayor and Corporation—joined in, it is stated, by Conservatives and Liberal Unionists—he delivered a short speech couched in equally general terms, in the course of which ha expressed a_hope that he might infer from his reception that the temperature of political diff- erences was going down. Lord Salisbury, in opening the new Constitutional Club at Scarborough, on Thurs- day, spoke of the advantages such institutions conferred on the party, and referred with satisfaction to the alli- ance between the Conservatives and Liberal Unionists, which boded well for the best interests of the country they loved.
